articles.title_orig: Costs above competition? Why US voters aren’t buying Trump’s China AI pitch
articles.title_zh: Costs above competition? Why US voters aren’t buying Trump’s China AI pitch
articles.content_orig:
Democratic victories and opposition to AI infrastructure highlight concerns over power bills, water use and the impact on local communities
Strong voter backlash in the US midterm elections against AI infrastructure projects, including data centres, indicates that framing the domestic buildout as key to competing with China failed to convince Americans and underscores the need to address local concerns, according to analysts.
“The argument that we need to build more data centres to win in AI against China no longer seems to have the kind of resonance it did before, if it ever did, frankly,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Centre.
Lizzi Lee, a fellow at the Asia Society Policy Institute, echoed that assessment, saying: “The lesson is that invoking China as a justification for tech and industrial investment is becoming less effective.”

articles.title_zh: China, US defence officials agree to improve ‘communication’ to reduce risks
articles.content_orig:
Military officials from two countries to work on promoting ‘effective’ crisis management after constructive meeting in Washington
US and Chinese defence officials met in Washington for the first meeting of a Crisis Communications and Prevention Working Group established under an agreement announced in September when leaders of the two nations met.
The two sides agreed on the importance of “advancing practical communication measures” to reduce risks between the US and China, according to a Pentagon readout of the meeting released Tuesday. Delegates also discussed “additional channels” to promote “effective” crisis management and ways to communicate “expediently and effectively”.

articles.title_orig: CVS to break up $117 billion business, separating pharmacies from insurance; shares fall
articles.title_zh: CVS to break up $117 billion business, separating pharmacies from insurance; shares fall
articles.content_orig:
CVS Health said Wednesday it is splitting into two companies, marking one of the largest shakeups in the healthcare industry. It’s a major reversal of the mergers that brought together the nation’s largest drugstore retailer along with health insurance giant Aetna and pharmacy benefit manager Caremark.
One company, which would house CVS’s 9,000 retail pharmacies, mail order pharmacy, specialty drug business and MinuteClinic, will be named CVS Pharmacy.
The other, comprising of Aetna, Caremark and two companies that CVS acquired that provide primary care and in-home health evaluations to senior citizens, will be called CVS Health in the interim.
The separation is expected to close in early 2028.
The breakup unwinds a strategy that began in 2007, when CVS merged with Caremark, which handles prescription benefits available to people with health insurance. In 2018, CVS acquired Aetna for $69 billion.
“We’re basically taking what I believe is one great company and making it two,” said CVS CEO David Joyner in a statement Wednesday.
The company split will have little impact on the way people shop at CVS – the company didn’t announce any closures as part of the news – nor will affect what patients pay for prescriptions.
Pharmacy benefit management businesses work on the backend, negotiating directly with drugmakers on the cost of prescription drugs. But CVS’s drugstores and Caremark insurance operate separately. Splitting into two companies won’t change how they function.
The split does, however, mark a major step back from the widespread trend to integrate various parts of the healthcare industry – including insurers, pharmacy benefit managers and providers – into massive conglomerates. That consolidation has come under attack from consumer advocates and state and federal lawmakers for wielding too much control of the sector, leading to higher costs for patients. Some members of Congress have called for breaking up the companies.
Also, health insurers have come under cost pressure because Americans are using more healthcare services. Meanwhile, lawmakers and regulators are seeking to reform the pharmacy benefit manager industry just as it contends with new players looking to chip away at the dominance of Caremark and other major PBMs.
Meanwhile, CVS’ retail business has been hampered by consumers shifting to online channels, where the company still lags leaders like Amazon, Michael Cherny, an analyst with Leerink Partners, wrote in a client note on Tuesday evening after reports of the split surfaced.
Cherny, who called the news “a complete shock,” wrote that CVS’ pharmacy business has been performing well so “perhaps the outlook for a standalone retail pharmacy (still with meaningful scale and leverage on its own) is stronger now than before.”
Joyner, who will lead the new CVS Health company, took over as CEO in 2024 in the wake of layoffs, store closings and poor stock performance.
Shares of CVS Health, which have risen since Joyner’s appointment, fell 12% in midday trading after initially ticking up in premarket trading. Shareholders will get shares of both companies in a tax-free transaction, according to the company.
CVS also reported higher third-quarter earnings and revenue Wednesday, due primarily to better results from its Health Care Benefits segment. The company also raised its earnings guidance for the rest of this year.
CVS has 9,000 locations across the United States, 800 of which operate “MinuteClinics” staffed by nurse practitioners and physician assistants. It has 30,000 pharmacists and 200,000 employees in its stores, the company said during an earnings call Wednesday.

articles.title_orig: A Lawsuit Says the McRib Is Lacking Something You Might Expect It to Have
articles.title_zh: A Lawsuit Says the McRib Is Lacking Something You Might Expect It to Have
articles.content_orig:
Oct. 31 (UPI) -- A federal judge on Friday allowed a lawsuit against McDonald's to move forward, alleging the fast food chain misleads customers into believing its popular McRib sandwich contains actual pork rib meat.
McDonald's had asked the court to dismiss a lawsuit in Chicago alleging consumer deception, fraud and unjust enrichment.
But U.S. District Judge April Perry ruled the lawsuit, filed by four customers in December 2025, could move forward, FOX Business reported.
First sold in 1981, the McRib features a boneless pork patty molded to resemble ribs. It is covered in barbecue sauce and served with onions and pickles.
The plaintiffs accuse McDonald's of using the sandwich's name and appearance to suggest that it contains rib meat, despite allegedly using cheaper portions of pork.
The lawsuit claims the McRib is made from ground pork products, including shoulder, heart, tripe and stomach, rather than meat taken from the ribs, according to KTLA .
McDonald's has denied the allegations.
One survey submitted in the case found that 72% of respondents believed the sandwich contained pork rib meat.
Another survey found 67% considered rib meat an important factor in their decision to buy the McRib.
The ruling comes as McDonald's brings back the McRib for another limited run.
The sandwich returned to participating restaurants Oct. 27 in locations including Los Angeles, Chicago, Miami, Dallas, Atlanta and Philadelphia.

articles.title_orig: Trump hand-picked Senate candidates. Republicans paid the price
articles.title_zh: Trump hand-picked Senate candidates. Republicans paid the price
articles.content_orig:
China, Canada, India and South Africa could gain fresh leverage in trade negotiations with Washington after Democrats seized control of both chambers of the US Congress, weakening President Donald Trump's political position amid growing discontent over the Iran war, rising consumer prices and his controversial trade tariffs.
The November 3 midterm elections saw Republicans lose their majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, with Democrats securing victories in Republican strongholds, including Texas, Kansas and South Carolina.
Republicans suffered the setback amid rising living costs, Trump's tariffs and the eight-month Iran war, which disrupted energy supplies and pushed Brent crude to $138.21 per barrel in April, its highest level since 2008, fuelling US inflation.
From what Business Insider Africa has gathered, the results could encourage America's trade rivals and dissatisfied partners to resist Washington's demands, delay investments and seek better trade deals as Trump will now have to answer to a Democrat-controlled Congress.
DON'T MISS: Despite warnings from China, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, Israel presses ahead with embassy plans in breakaway African territory near Red Sea
China is among the countries that could use Trump's weakened political position to push for more favourable trade terms, particularly as Beijing seeks to recover exports lost to American tariffs.
The impact of those restrictions is reflected in US trade figures, which show that America's goods trade deficit with China narrowed from $295.5 billion in 2024 to $202.1 billion in 2025.
With a temporary trade truce approaching expiration in January 2027, Beijing could seek lower tariffs and fewer technology restrictions, calculating that Trump faces greater political resistance to another trade war.
Saul Eslake, an economist at Corinna Economic Advisory in Australia, believes China could take advantage of the changing political balance in Washington.
"Xi Jinping will recognize that Trump's authority has been greatly weakened by these results, and will no doubt be thinking about ways of exploiting that," Eslake told Reuters.
Although Beijing has not publicly indicated plans to exploit Trump's political setback, China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning described the elections as an internal US matter, saying the country would continue managing differences and expanding cooperation with Washington.
DON'T MISS: Two Chinese mining firms pull out of Kenya’s rare earth and niobium extraction race as three American companies stand their ground among five remaining bidders
Canada could also find greater support in Washington after months of difficult trade negotiations between Prime Minister Mark Carney and Trump's administration over tariffs and market access.
Talks stalled in August after Ottawa rejected American demands, while tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium and other products continued to strain relations between the neighbouring economies.
In an October 30 interview with POLITICO, Carney indicated that Canada would rather wait for another American president than accept an unfavourable agreement.
Asked whether Canada could hold out until Trump's successor took office, he replied: "Well, if that's what it takes, yeah."
His position could receive support from Democrats, particularly Senator Ron Wyden, a senior member of the Senate Finance Committee, who has called for removing tariffs on Canadian goods because of their impact on businesses and consumers.
DON'T MISS: European nation stops foreign workers and students from South Africa, Ghana, India and other countries from applying for residence permits inside the country
India could gain negotiating flexibility as New Delhi seeks better trade terms while American consumers face higher prices on imported goods.
Washington imposed tariffs of up to 50% on Indian products in 2025 amid trade disputes and disagreements over India's purchases of Russian oil. The restrictions affected textiles, jewellery and footwear, increasing costs for American importers.
The countries agreed in February 2026 to a framework reducing tariffs on most Indian goods to 18%, but negotiations remain unfinished.
Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said the agreement had reached the final drafting stage, although New Delhi would proceed only if it secured an advantage over competing exporters.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman also acknowledged in October that further concessions would be "very, very difficult" for both sides.
The Democratic victory could encourage India to resist additional demands as Trump faces greater scrutiny of his trade policies from the Democrat-controlled Congress.
South Africa faces a trade setback after Washington announced on November 2 that it would remove the country from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) on January 1, 2027, following months of diplomatic tensions over Pretoria's domestic and foreign policies.
The decision threatens preferential access for South African exports, including vehicles, citrus fruits and wine, adding to existing trade pressures after the country's agricultural exports to the US fell by 28% in the second quarter of 2026.
President Cyril Ramaphosa previously urged South Africans to prepare for possible exclusion, saying: "We should not go out and jump off tall buildings and think that this is the end of the world."
However, in a sharp reversal of his earlier cautious stance, Ramaphosa welcomed the Democratic victory on November 4, saying: "We have seen that the Democrats have taken control of the Senate and of the House, and the people of America have spoken."
He added that the results could introduce "a new era in world relations", raising hopes of improved ties with Washington.
"We're hoping that, on a bilateral basis, there will be a coming together of minds, where we will find a proper path forward on geopolitics as well as on trade matters and investment matters," Ramaphosa said.

articles.title_orig: Israel's president takes first steps on building new government after accepting election results
articles.title_zh: Israel's president takes first steps on building new government after accepting election results
articles.content_orig:
Move comes after attorney general blocks Shin Bet call to interrogate politicians from Palestinian-led parties
Israel’s election commission on Wednesday confirmed the final results of last week’s vote that stripped Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition of its governing majority, rejecting claims of mass fraud promoted by the prime minister.
The main challenger, Gadi Eisenkot, said Netanyahu had launched a “pogrom against democracy” in attempting to hold on to power by discrediting valid votes and weaponising security forces against parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel .
Hours earlier, Israel’s attorney general said she had blocked a demand from the Shin Bet security service to interrogate senior politicians from the Palestinian-led parties because she had not been presented with any evidence of wrongdoing.
“In a country governed by the rule of law, neither citizens nor elected officials can be interrogated without evidence that justifies doing so,” Gali Baharav-Miara said in a statement, after Haaretz reported on the attempt to target four politicians.
Election authorities on Wednesday presented the final results to the president, Isaac Herzog, after rejecting allegations they had been tainted by large-scale foreign interference and voter fraud.
“The review found no evidence of irregularities that compromised the integrity of the election or affected its results,” the Central Elections Committee said in a statement.
The body’s chair, Noam Sohlberg, said some “suspicions” were still under investigation but “they do not cast doubt on the election as a whole or justify delaying the election results”.
When the results were handed over, Herzog denounced racist attacks on Palestinian citizens who had turned out to vote at historic rates.
“I condemn the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently,” he said. “I hold Arab society in Israel in great respect. I value its contribution to the country in every area of life, and its desire to integrate.”
Herzog will play a key role in the formation of the next government by choosing which politician has the first chance to create a coalition. He is expected to name Eisenkot, and the announcement could come as early as Thursday evening.
A former leader of the Israeli military who lost his son fighting in Gaza, Eisenkot has secured the public support of all of the Jewish Israeli opposition parties. Palestinian-led parties have said their priority is removing Netanyahu, so they are expected to back him as the strongest contender to achieve that.
However, negotiations could take weeks and Eisenkot warned of ongoing attempts to undermine trust in the election results. He accused Netanyahu of weaponising the security services against domestic opponents in an effort to hold on to power.
“The employees of the Ministry of Defense, law enforcement and the civil service in Israel are servants of the state, not the king,” he said in a statement. “Woe to anyone who abuses their authority and role for political considerations.”
The Shin Bet chief, David Zini, handpicked for the role by Netanyahu, had ordered the interrogations and sought to classify the investigation as a security file, which would have allowed harsher conditions including barring the politicians from having legal counsel.
Nadav Eyal, an Israeli journalist and commentator, said the public should brace for more extreme attempts to dismiss election results and discredit the leading opposition parties.
“The groundwork is steadily being laid for violence,” he wrote on X. “What you’re hearing breaking right now is the foundation of the legal and governmental orders in Israel.”
Netanyahu presided over a racist campaign targeting Palestinian citizens of Israel – about 20% of the population – and on election day began promoting the unfounded accusations of mass fraud now rejected by election authorities.
Ahmad Tibi, one of the most prominent and effective Palestinian politicians, was reportedly among those the Shin Bet sought to interrogate. He responded to the latest allegations, as news broke of sweeping victories for Democrats in the US midterms, with a swipe at Netanyahu’s fear of democracy.
“[The] attorney general is checking suspicion of ties between the Joint List and Democrats in the US,” Tibi wrote in a social media post. “According to the suspicion, in both cases the same sophisticated method was employed: people arrived in droves at the polling stations, cast a slip, and went home.”

articles.title_orig: Google Tries to Walk Back Controversial School AI Policy Following Political Backlash
articles.title_zh: Google Tries to Walk Back Controversial School AI Policy Following Political Backlash
articles.content_orig:
Students using Google software in schools will not be allowed to use Google search unless their school system also provides them access to artificial intelligence tools
Students using Google software in the classroom will not be allowed to access the company's search engine unless their school system also opts in to artificial intelligence tools , the tech giant said Tuesday.
The Mountain View, California, company has been facing pushback from educators, child development experts and parents over the use of its technology in schools, with the backlash heating up since it announced in August that it had turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students who use Google Classroom.
On Tuesday, the company said that practice would no longer be the default option for school administrators and that opting out of AI tools would also mean losing access to Google search.
Access to Google's AI features — Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Gemini in Classroom — as well as Google search will be automatically turned off for K-12 student accounts until “school administrators explicitly turn them on,” Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager of education, said in a blog post .
“We believe schools should have control over AI in their classrooms and in providing administrators with controls to help them manage their approach,” Phillips wrote.
Google is by far the dominant provider of education technology for U.S. schools. Worldwide, the company says 150 million students and teachers use its Google Classroom platform and many students use school-provided Chromebook computers.
Google faced an outcry in August when it switched on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students. Until August, Google had only allowed Gemini to be turned on for students 18 or older.
Tuesday's announcement was met with swift criticism from educators and policymakers.
“Google is using its search monopoly to coerce schools into adopting AI. This highlights the danger of allowing an unregulated monopolist to control an essential service,” wrote Lina Khan, former chair of the Federal Trade Commission, on social media. “As the public increasingly pushes back against the use of AI in schools, Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”
Messages seeking additional comment from Google were left on Tuesday.
New York City and Los Angeles, home to the nation's biggest school districts, have issued temporary bans on generative AI tools in elementary and middle schools as they assess AI use and safety and develop policies on its use.
Many students already use AI to help with school and homework, but the technology has also made it easier to cheat and find quick, easy answers to questions instead of thinking critically. And experts have raised questions about how access to AI is affecting children’s brain development .
Josh Golin, executive director of children's advocacy group Fairplay, said Google's attempt to “strong-arm schools into using its AI products is likely to backfire.” He said Google's technology in schools is not about learning but about “developing lifetime brand loyalty” for its products.
“Because AI isn’t safe for kids and undermines education and critical thinking, schools should turn off Google’s AI tools the minute that option becomes available," Golin said in a statement.
Rather than fret about losing access to search, Golin urged schools to turn off not just AI but also Google, and "use this opportunity to help students find more privacy-protective alternatives for search, as well as ways to do more substantive research beyond search and click.”

Renewable-energy stocks rose on Wednesday, with First Solar (FSLR), Sunrun (RUN), and Enphase Energy (ENPH) posting strong gains.
Shares of Vistra Corp. (VST) and Constellation Energy (CEG) fell sharply on Wednesday after Democrats secured projected majorities in both the U.S. House and Senate and Texas elected Democrat Gina Hinojosa as governor.
Vistra traded 15% lower at the time of writing, on track for its worst day since January 2025, if the losses hold. Constellation, meanwhile, declined 9%, as investors worry about regulatory uncertainty for data-center-driven power demand.

KeyBanc analyst Sophie Karp downgraded Vistra to 'Sector Weight' from 'Overweight' and removed the firm's prior price target on the stock. Karp stated that a Democratic sweep in Texas "will come as a negative surprise to investors," noting that Governor-elect Hinojosa campaigned on a stricter moratorium on data-center development. The firm expects both Vistra and Constellation Energy to face negative effects from the resulting policy uncertainty, with Vistra carrying the greatest exposure because of its substantial presence in the Texas power market.
Hinojosa's victory marked the first Democratic win in the Texas governor's race since 1990. She has advocated an immediate pause on new data-center construction, an end to related tax incentives, and stronger local controls over water and electricity use.
Outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott had already ordered pauses on certain grid connections and environmental permits for data centers amid public concerns, but Hinojosa has called for more permanent and expansive restrictions. Texas accounts for a large share of planned U.S. data-center capacity. Vistra's third-quarter results on November 6 could offer more detail on the company's own estimates of regulatory shifts, with Constellation's earnings report following shortly afterward.
The selloff extended beyond the two independent power producers. GE Vernova (GEV) and Vertiv (VRT), companies tied to the data center infrastructure boom, each declined around 10%, while data-center operators such as CoreWeave and Applied Digital also weakened on expectations of greater congressional scrutiny.
In contrast, renewable-energy stocks rose, with First Solar (FSLR), Sunrun (RUN), and Enphase Energy (ENPH) posting strong gains on hopes that Democrats in Congress could support federal incentives for clean power.
On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around CEG stock was 'bearish' at the time of writing, while sentiment around VST was 'neutral.'
A Stocktwits user highlighted that Vistra's CEO James Burke bought shares of the company worth about $1 million at an average price of $135 per share in late August and September, signaling confidence in the share price.
Another user termed the VST stock selloff as overdone and urged buying the dip.
While VST stock has dropped about 25% year-to-date, CEG has dropped about 31%.

articles.title_orig: E.l.f. Beauty posts 51% sales increase, raises full-year guidance
articles.title_zh: E.l.f. Beauty posts 51% sales increase, raises full-year guidance
articles.content_orig:
E.l.f. Beauty on Wednesday blew past Wall Street expectations as it posted a 51% increase in net sales in its second fiscal quarter.
The beauty company said it saw its 31st consecutive quarter of net sales growth, attributing the streak to strong performance across its portfolio. The revenue spike was driven by both retail and e-commerce channels across the U.S. and internationally, the company added.
"The thing I'm most pleased about is we saw strength across our entire portfolio," CEO Tarang Amin told CNBC in an interview. "Every one of our brands contributed strong growth this quarter."
Amin added that E.l.f. is the most-searched brand on TikTok Shop and the No. 2 brand in cosmetics on the platform. The company also said it saw strong results for Rhode, the skincare brand it acquired last year.
The company raised its full fiscal-year guidance following the better-than-anticipated quarter. It now expects net sales in the range of $2 billion to $2.03 billion, compared with a previous range of between $1.94 billion and $1.97 billion. It also upped its adjusted EBITDA projection to a range of $421 million to $427 million from between $401 million and $407 million.
E.l.f. said it now expects adjusted earnings per share for the year to come in between $3.82 and $3.86, exceeding prior guidance of between $3.50 and $3.55 per share. It's also expecting a net income range of $231 million to $233 million, up from a previous range of $212 million to $215 million.
It had already raised its guidance last quarter after outperforming its expectations.
Amin said the company is "very bullish" on the holiday season, expecting high sales through the end of the year.
Here's how the company performed in its second fiscal quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
For the period ended Sept. 30, E.l.f. reported net income of $30.03 million, or 50 cents per share, up significantly from roughly $3 million, or 5 cents per share, the year prior.
Net sales grew 51% to $520.8 million.
E.l.f. also saw significant growth in its international channels, with business up 165%. Amin told CNBC that only 25% of the company's business is outside of the U.S. and that it has a "tremendous opportunity" to build on that momentum.
The company also said its gross margin increased 1.6% during the quarter, including a 0.3% benefit from tariff refunds. Amin previously said the retailer planned to fully reinvest that money into pricing and marketing to continue driving growth.
Though E.l.f. received most of its refunds in its first fiscal quarter, some of those funds flowed through the second quarter, and the company expects to receive a yearly total of around $55 million. Amin told CNBC on Wednesday that the company lowered the price of about 10% of its units by $1 because of the tariff benefits.
"We're seeing great unit momentum based on that," he said.

SANTA CRUZ, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--
Joby Aviation, Inc. (NYSE:JOBY), a company developing electric air taxis for commercial passenger service, today issued its Third Quarter 2026 Shareholder Letter detailing the company’s operational and financial results for the quarter ending September 30, 2026. The company will host a live audio webcast of its conference call to discuss the results at 2:00 p.m. PT (5:00 p.m. ET) today.
This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20261104420012/en/
Joby’s all- electric, vertical take-off and landing air taxi flies over Tampa, Florida, on Oct. 29 during the state’s first eIPP flights. (Photo: Joby Aviation)
Commenting on Joby’s third quarter results, JoeBen Bevirt, founder and CEO , said:
“This quarter, we made important progress on the fifth and final stage of certification, completing a wide range of ‘for credit’ testing with the FAA. We significantly increased manufacturing output while improving efficiency, and demonstrated our electric air taxi in key early U.S. markets through the White House-backed eIPP program. Our J208 aircraft also completed what we believe to be the first fully autonomous flight of a civilian aircraft across the United States, and this morning we announced an expansion of our autonomy-focused contracts with the U.S. Air Force to nearly $37 million.”
“Our core mission is - and always has been - to bring electric vertical flight to passengers around the world. We designed our aircraft from the ground up for that mission, and our engineering, manufacturing and certification efforts are focused on bringing it to market. The progress we’re making gives me every confidence that Joby will continue to lead the way.”
Joby’s current outlook incorporates investment toward certification of our eVTOL aircraft, expansion of manufacturing, and advancement of commercial preparations including participation in the U.S. eVTOL Integration Pilot Program. The company increased its full year 2026 total revenue outlook to a range of $135 million to $140 million. For the second half of 2026, Joby anticipates use of cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments to be between $385 million and $415 million.
Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Webcast Details What: Joby Aviation Third Quarter 2026 Financial Results Webcast When: Wednesday, November 4, 2026 Time: 2:00 p.m. PT (5:00 p.m. ET) Webcast: Upcoming Events section of the company website .
If unable to attend the webcast, to listen by phone, please dial 1-877-407-9719 or 1-201-378-4906. A replay of the webcast will be available on the company website following the event.
Joby Aviation, Inc. (NYSE: JOBY) is a next-generation aviation company based in California. Its aircraft, propulsion and autonomy technologies span both commercial aviation and defense applications. Joby also operates Blade, a leading urban air mobility business providing passenger transportation services in the United States and Europe. Joby intends to operate its fast, quiet and convenient air taxi service in cities around the world and sell its aircraft to other operators and partners. To learn more, visit www.jobyaviation.com .

articles.title_orig: French blood banks targeted by refrigerator cyberattack
articles.title_zh: French blood banks targeted by refrigerator cyberattack
articles.content_orig:
Blood banks in France were included among cyberattacks that hit refrigeration systems in several European countries on Sunday and Monday, French authorities said on Wednesday.
The French Blood Establishment (EFS) said that a " cybersecurity incident" targeted a refrigeration service provider affecting control systems at three cold storage sites for plasma and blood samples.
The cyberattack attempted to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but it was warded off before any damage could be done. The plasma in the affected refrigerators was transferred or secured, the EFS said.
"No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost," the EFS said in a statement, adding that its distribution operations were not interrupted.
The cyberattack was first reported on Wednesday by the French weekly newspaper Le Canard Enchaine , which said the temperatures had been programmed to reach a boiling 110 C (230 F), rather than -30 Celsius (minus 22 Fahrenheit).
"Monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the anomalies, allowing staff to take action to ensure that no blood products or samples were compromised," the EFS said.
France's cybersecurity agency and Health Ministry said an investigation is underway, but did not indicate who could have been responsible.
The Health Ministry said Wednesday that remote access to the affected refrigerators was disabled, and credited monitoring and alarm systems with ensuring the safety of blood supplies.
Coolworld, the company supplying the refrigeration equipment, said the vulnerability was related to a component from a "third-party supplier and was outside Coolworld's direct control."
On Sunday and Monday, a cyberattack targeted refrigeration systems at supermarkets in several European countries, including France and Germany, destroying large quantities of frozen food.
It was reminiscent of a similar attack three weeks ago targeting refrigeration systems at dozens of French supermarkets.
The attacks have cost supermarkets millions of euros in wasted food.
On Wednesday, Dutch supermarket chain Ahold Delhaize said it expects the cyberattack in October to reduce quarterly sales by as much as €250 million ($281 million).
"While most of the disruption was contained within two weeks, work continues to fully restore our normal operations," CEO Franz Muller said.

articles.title_orig: A nationwide backlash against data centers erupts at the polls
articles.title_zh: A nationwide backlash against data centers erupts at the polls
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
A strong showing by Democrats in Texas swept Gina Hinojosa into office as the state's first Democratic governor since 1990 in a contest closely watched by Big Tech companies.
Texas is considered a bellwether for government restrictions on AI data centers and was just one place where deep voter unease over the build-out was on display. Voters across the country passed a series of local ballot measures aimed at restricting construction in the years ahead.
Hinojosa, Texas's first Latina governor, has pledged to impose a moratorium on data center construction in Texas, which accounts for more than 25% of planned US capacity by 2030.
"I want to say something to the powerful people who have gotten very comfortable running this state," she told supporters in her victory speech . "The voters have delivered a mandate for change, and it is change they will get."
Her victory was one of a series of wins for Democrats in Texas. The party is also on track to take control of the Texas House , which would give Hinojosa more power to follow through on restrictions even as the state Senate appears set to remain under Republican control.
"We view the Texas gubernatorial race as particularly important for the next leg of the AI trade," wrote Raymond James's Ed Mills in a pre-election note saying that a strong Democratic showing there "could signal a broader electoral wave while increasing concerns about data center moratoriums and more restrictive AI regulation in the nation's largest planned data center development."
Bank of America called the race "one of the highest impact elections for the entire utility sector."
Hinojosa made opposition to data center construction a central part of her campaign, charging in one ad that Gov. Greg Abbott "works for" Elon Musk.
She staked out plans for a moratorium on new data center construction, stricter regulations on water and power usage, and an end to tax breaks.
Abbott was seeking his fourth term as governor and said last year he wanted Texas to be the "epicenter of AI development."
More recently, he announced a moratorium of his own and said he would support more stringent requirements on power and water usage. Hinojosa immediately charged that Abbott's new proposals amounted to an "election year pause."
Tobin Marcus of Wolfe Research said Texas "is the one state with enough scale and enough difference between the candidates that it could make a real difference."
The race reflected a national mood that has turned sharply against data centers in recent months.
NBC exit polls on Tuesday showed that 57% of voters felt "AI will do more to hurt society" compared to just 24% who said it would help.
A UMass Amherst Poll in September also found nearly two-thirds of Americans oppose AI data center construction in their communities, with just 11% of voters welcoming them
On Tuesday, voters weighed in on data center ballot measures in contests spanning 13 states, from Arkansas to Wisconsin.
One tracker counted 28 measures before voters to limit data centers. On Wednesday morning, with votes still being counted, virtually every one was on track to pass. In Ohio alone, voters in at least 14 municipalities passed bans or other restrictions .
In the Ohio Senate race, voters elected Democrat Sherrod Brown, who, like Hinojosa, made opposition to data center construction a key part of his campaign message.
"I do not work for the utility companies, I do not work for data centers," Brown said as he declared victory on Tuesday night .
Even Elon Musk seemed to acknowledge the dour public sentiment toward data centers. He quipped in a post early Wednesday as the results became clear, "data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now."
This story has been updated.
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: Treasury Yields Fall on Election Results, Cheaper Oil
articles.title_zh: Treasury Yields Fall on Election Results, Cheaper Oil
articles.content_orig:
The electoral sweep by Democrats on Tuesday night injects a new, unstable dynamic into the single biggest political risk to financial markets in the coming year: the debt limit . Unless a defeated Republican Party makes a swift and unlikely show of unity to take the issue off the table in its last few weeks in power, the protracted fight that will unfold is set to be nastier than ever, adding volatility to an already shaky bond market.
Follow CNBC's live coverage of the 2026 midterm election results
Past episodes of brinkmanship around the need to raise the government's borrowing limit have involved Republicans in Congress demanding budget cuts from a Democratic president as the price of their vote. This time it will almost certainly be the left seeking concessions from the right.
The debt limit is the definition of a must-pass bill, even more than issues like funding the government and the defense budget. That makes it potentially the one real chance the new Democratic majority in Congress has to extract concessions from a president who is already pledging to veto their agenda. Markets will hate the entire process, even if — as many expect — it ends in compromise.
Because it is Democrats who hold the leverage, unlike past episodes, the ultimate agreement is more likely to increase government spending than lower it. With high bond yields weighing on the economy, and Americans expecting action from a newly empowered Democratic opposition, the fight could be particularly damaging.
Many in the markets are stuck on the outdated idea that Democrats are less assertive than Republicans, said Aniket Shah, head of the Washington policy team at the investment bank Jefferies.
"They have this sort of mental image of Biden-Harris 2024," said Shah. "I don't think they realize how aggressively Democrats plan to take 2027."
The debt ceiling is a quirk of the congressional budgeting process. It stops the government from borrowing funds that Congress has already ordered federal agencies to spend. And because Congress has run deficits for decades — this year at $1.99 trillion — the pile of debt periodically bumps into the debt ceiling.
Congress last set the limit in 2025, when it gave the Treasury Department the authority to borrow $41.1 trillion. The Treasury is likely to hit its maximum borrowing capacity by midsummer, according to the Bipartisan Policy Center , a nonprofit that tracks the issue.
The Treasury can use budgeting techniques to extend the so-called X-date, when the U.S. would no longer be able to meet all its obligations, to sometime in the fourth quarter of 2027, according to Wall Street estimates.
A few technical hiccups aside, the U.S. has never meaningfully breached the debt limit. The results of the U.S. missing payments would be chaotic as damage ripples out across the financial system into the global economy. U.S. default would immediately call into question trillions in Treasury securities that are the lifeblood of the global financial system. Damaging them could send the U.S. and global economies into an economic tailspin with no obvious means of recovery.
Because the stakes are so high, Shah and many others on Wall Street have come to believe that the episode will produce volatility but will ultimately be resolved in compromise.
Fights under former Presidents Barack Obama and Joe Biden saw Republican congressional majorities use the issue to ram through spending reductions. (The 2025 raise was less contentious, because Republicans held Congress and the presidency. It was passed along party lines.)
Still, the risk-taking in those episodes contributed to ratings firms' decisions to downgrade U.S. debt — and could again.
President Donald Trump has called for Republicans to resolve the issue in the next few weeks, before the new Democratic-majority Congress is seated.
That isn't likely. The 2025 debt limit increase only passed because it was tied to a package of tax cuts and other policy changes. Republican debt hawks complained but held their noses.
Republicans may attempt to raise the limit in the coming lame-duck session under a budgeting procedure called reconciliation, which would allow them to move ahead without Democrats' votes. But success would require unity among a fractured, fleeting Republican majority that also faces several other more pressing priorities.
The most likely path toward raising the debt limit is the incoming Democratic majority negotiating another temporary fix with Trump. But they aren't going to make it easy. The president has occasionally made noises about making deals, but the political incentives ahead of the 2028 presidential election are for both sides to dig in.
"[Democrats] are going to want to embarrass the White House, and they're going to want to get leverage," Shah said. Democrats will use that to push to reverse cuts to Medicaid spending passed in 2025 and to try to restore healthcare spending, he said.
Democrats could also seek to tie the debt limit to restraining signature Trump policies, such as limiting the war with Iran or rolling back tariffs, analysts at Goldman Sachs said in a research note Wednesday.
Another potential compromise being considered in some corners of Washington is for Democrats to tie an increase in the corporate tax rate to a debt limit raise, said George Pollack, senior U.S. analyst with Signum Global Advisors. Trump has shown he can be surprisingly flexible on similar issues, Pollack noted.
That is what will make this debt limit fight different. In the past, Republicans used it to try to win spending reductions they couldn't get through regular budget negotiations. Now Democrats will broaden it out into an all-purpose hostage. That effort is far more likely to raise overall government spending than cut it. "There's a very weird irony here," said Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at PGIM, an asset manager.
The path to compromise will likely be rocky. Sockin believes it may turn out like the 2025 government shutdown. That was the longest government-wide shutdown in history, even though Democrats weren't in control of either chamber of Congress. This time they will have even more power.
If the fight extends beyond the X-date, missing debt payments could do serious damage to the financial system.
"It's not our base case, but we think the risk is higher than ever that you could get a technical default from the government," Sockin said. That would see the U.S. miss a payment, even if the government eventually makes it up.
That would still hurt. "You'll get more downgrades to the U.S. sovereign, and those might bite more this time," Sockin said. Yields on longer-term Treasurys would rise to account for added uncertainty.
Crossing the red line could prompt a "very negative reaction in equity markets," he said.
The coming months will show just how close Democrats are willing to get to that line.

articles.title_orig: Serbia detains police officers over alleged use of force against protesters
articles.title_zh: Serbia detains police officers over alleged use of force against protesters
articles.content_orig:
Interior ministry claims suspects tortured and intimidated protesters detained in garage of government compound
Serbian authorities detained nine active police officers and one former officer on Wednesday for ⁠allegedly using excessive force against detainees during anti-corruption protests last year in Belgrade, the country’s interior ministry ⁠said.
Anti-corruption protests swept ⁠across Serbia, ​a candidate for European Union membership, in 2025 and 2026 after 16 people died when a concrete canopy ⁠on a renovated railway station in the city of Novi Sad collapsed on 1 November 2024.
The protests ultimately ⁠resulted in the ouster of the populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which is ​loyal to former president Aleksandar Vučić, in ‌an 25 October ‌snap parliamentary election by the leaderless Student List.
The ministry said in a ‌statement that the suspects, who served in an elite unit, tortured and intimidated several people detained in the garage of the government compound in downtown Belgrade on 14-15 August 2025.
“By the use of force and threats, (they) inflicted great pain and severe suffering on a larger ‌number of persons, intending to obtain information from them and intimidating and unlawfully punishing them,” the statement said.
The ministry provided ​only the initials of the officers and former officer who were detained. The news marked the first big arrests in connection with violence against the protesters who took to the streets over the past two years.
Police ⁠used teargas, crowd-control vehicles and stun grenades to disperse ​crowds during the ​protests.
Dozens of students and activists ​who took part in the protests accused police of ​excessive use of ‌force that ​resulted in injuries ​and psychological trauma.
Serbian students, activists, opposition politicians and rights watchdogs have accused Vučić and the SNS of political violence, pressure against media, ties to organised crime and rampant corruption. Vučić and his allies deny the accusations.

articles.title_orig: Stock market today: Dow rallies 1,500 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq gain after Democrats win control of Congress
articles.title_zh: Stock market today: Dow rallies 1,500 points, S&P 500 and Nasdaq gain after Democrats win control of Congress
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks jumped on Wednesday after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in a seismic midterm election, paving the way for a divided government.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 3%, or over 1,500 points, marking its best single-day performance since President Trump paused a sweeping tariff rollout in April 2025. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) climbed 1.6%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) traded up by 1.4% amid a post-election relief rally.
Markets swiftly repriced a Democratic sweep of the House and Senate — and the potential for ballot measures and newly elected officials to restrict data center construction . Chip stocks, including Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Micron ( MU ), fell. Meanwhile, other parts of the tech sector offset some of those losses, with Apple ( AAPL ) and Microsoft ( MSFT ) each hitting all-time highs.
Oil prices plunged as the midterm election outcome also raised hopes for an end to the war in the Middle East. Brent crude oil futures ( BZ=F ) dropped 8% to around $95 per barrel.
Investors will also be watching in the coming weeks for policy actions on housing and pharmaceuticals in the aftermath of the election. As Yahoo Finance's Jared Blikre pointed out on Tuesday , midterm elections have a history of shaping stock performance in the near term but don't tend to move markets much over the long term.
On the economic front, ISM and S&P data showed that US services activity expanded at a slower pace in October as businesses continued to grapple with elevated costs. Private-sector hiring , meanwhile, continued to show strength in October as an ADP report indicated "pretty solid job growth."
Earnings continue to roll in. AMD ( AMD ) posted a Q3 earnings beat , while McDonald's ( MCD ) grappled with slowing same-store sales growth . Duolingo ( DUOL ) stock soared over 30% on strong user growth.
US stocks rallied Wednesday after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress, as investors embraced the prospect of divided government and rotated into several of the market's biggest technology names.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) rose 3%, marking its best single-day performance since President Trump paused a sweeping tariff rollout in April 2025.
Meanwhile, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) gained 1.5%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) climbed 1.4%.
Oil prices plunged amid the rally in stocks, with West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) falling more than 7.7% below $90 a barrel.
Duolingo ( DUOL ) stock has recovered nearly all of its year-to-date losses after a strong earnings report eased concerns about the company's growth. Shares of the language learning app are up nearly 30% on the day.
In the third quarter, Duolingo reported that its daily active users (DAUs) rose 29% year over year to 64.9 million. Paid subscribers for the language learning platform grew 14% annually to 13.1 million.
Investors also cheered management's note that the company will be "gradually leaning more into monetization in ways that preserve the quality of our free experience."
"In our view, the quarter begins to address the primary investor concern following second-quarter results: whether accelerating engagement can translate into stronger monetization," William Blair analysts led by Ralph Schackart wrote in a note. "DAU growth accelerated for a second consecutive quarter, subscription bookings reaccelerated meaningfully, and management expects paid-subscriber growth to bottom in a couple of quarters as the stronger bookings trajectory flows through revenue."
The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) climbed on Wednesday, powered by cyclical and defensive stocks.
Consumer Discretionary, which houses e-commerce giant Amazon ( AMZN ), led the gains, followed closely by Communications Services, which includes tech giant Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ). Shares of Amazon rallied 7% while Alphabet rose more than 4%.
Financials ( XLF ) also rallied, along with defensive sectors like Consumer Staples( XLP ), Real Estate ( XLRE ), and Health Care ( XLV ).
Investors continued to rotate out of tech, even as it was up modestly on Wednesday. Political headwinds for the AI buildout and tumbling oil prices gave way to breadth outside semiconductor stocks, which have been the high fliers this year.
Wall Street's post-midterm party has two no-shows: the AI/chip trade and oil, which is having a far worse time.
West Texas Intermediate crude ( CL=F ) is back under $90 a barrel. It has given up about $15 since Friday's $104 close and is on pace for its worst week since April 2020. The slide came as traders bet on an end to the Iran war after Tuesday's elections.
Brent ( BZ=F ) is near a two-month low. Gasoline futures ( RB=F ) are on track for their lowest close since March 10, which is welcome news for anyone driving to Thanksgiving dinner. Energy stocks ( XLE ) are down more than 5%, with refiners taking the biggest hit.
Still, crude remains about 50% above where it started the year. US diesel stockpiles are at their lowest since 2003, and the Wells Fargo Investment Institute says gasoline and diesel supplies "remain constrained by the war."
Nationwide's Mark Hackett says oil is retreating "on hopes for a deescalation in the Iran conflict, even as the diplomatic signals remain ambiguous."
Watch whether WTI settles under $90 at 2:30 p.m. ET.
Voters on Tuesday delivered a stunning rebuke to the Trump agenda, but markets produced a referendum of their own — on the president's eponymous stock, Hamza Shaban reports:
Trump Media & Technology Group ( DJT ) stock, the home of the president's Truth Social platform, plunged over 12% during morning trading Wednesday. The ticker has served as a bellwether of the president's power, reflecting his outsized influence over all things politics, and his ability to attract capital and attention.
But the election results have shifted the balance of power. Democratic victories in battleground states and formerly Trump-voting districts have shattered the GOP's trifecta hold on Washington. And they have called into question Trump's own standing and effectiveness as party leader, chief executive, and business mogul.
Bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) jumped 3%, and ethereum ( ETH-USD ) also rallied on Wednesday after Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress, even as the midterm outcome could complicate the crypto industry's efforts to pass favorable legislation.
Bitcoin touched a six-week low before recovering to just above $80,000, moving back above its 50-day moving average. Ethereum also rallied, gaining 7% to trade above $2,400 as US equities broadly rallied and investors went risk-on.
Uber ( UBER ) reported third quarter results on Wednesday that topped estimates, but rising costs and weakness in the Middle East are expected to hit Q4 profit performance, Yahoo Finance's Pras Subramanian reports:
Uber stock rose 7% anyway.
Uber forecast fourth quarter adjusted ​EPS of $0.95 to $0.99, below estimates of $1.06. The company said the Middle East conflict was a 75-basis-point drag on mobility bookings and could be 100 basis points in Q4.
"Elevated fuel prices and tighter driver availability weighed on supply growth in several international markets," CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said in a statement.

articles.title_orig: Mother and daughter killed in grizzly bear attack, Canadian authorities confirm
articles.title_zh: Mother and daughter killed in grizzly bear attack, Canadian authorities confirm
articles.content_orig:
Conservation officers say more than one bear may have been involved in attack on women near their home
Search teams in Canada have discovered the body of a 20-year-old woman and confirmed that both she and her mother were killed in an attack that conservation officers now believe could have involved multiple grizzly bears.
Late on Tuesday, conservation officers in British Columbia said the two women, who were reported missing over the weekend, were located near a trail a short distance from their home.
The discovery has shaken a community where, earlier in the year, a grizzly attacked a group of schoolchildren and their teachers.
“Our thoughts are with the families of the victims during this tragic time,” Inspector Jeff Tyre of the British Columbia Conservation Officer Service said in a video posted online. Tyre later said the conservation service was investigating the possibility that more than one bear was involved in the fatal attack.
“We appreciate people’s concerns and the desire to assist but it is critical the public stay out of the area – both due to the danger and to allow officers to do their work,” he said.
Jenny Balcarras, an art therapist, and her daughter Selah Reed were reported missing by relatives over the weekend. A family member posted on Facebook about them, later updating it after the conservation service announced the suspected attack to indicate that their vehicle had been found at a trailhead near Bella Coola, British Columbia. Balcarras’s remains were found first and Reed was located a day later.
A fundraiser for Balcarras started by her family mourned a woman who had recently moved to Bella Coola, a community of roughly 2,100 people, for a new job and “to start a new chapter” of her life. She leaves behind three adult children and a grandchild.
“[Jenny] was working toward building a future and had not yet had the opportunity to establish savings or put aside funds to help her family with unexpected expenses such as these,” wrote relative Mary Melissa Smith. “Tragically, no one could have anticipated that her family would be faced with such an unimaginable loss.”
The family also mourned 20-year-old Selah, who had her “whole life ahead of her” before the attack.
“She was only beginning her journey into adulthood, making this loss even more heartbreaking,” wrote Smith.
Both Balcarras and Reed had lived in communities in remote and rugged parts of the province, as well as time in Alaska.
The suspected attack happened at the Snooka West trail area, about 8km (5 miles) east of Bella Coola, on the province’s central coast.
Bella Coola, which sits at the end of a fjord along the province’s central coast, is a remote location, and abundant food sources mean that grizzly bears are a common sight in the region, which is informally known as the Great Bear rainforest.
Grizzly attacks in the province are exceedingly rare, but last November, 11 people, some as young as nine years old, were injured when a grizzly emerged from the forest near 4 Mile, a Nuxalk community, and attacked a school group on a lunch break alongside a walking trail. Despite an extensive search, the bear was never located.
Samuel Schooner, elected chief of the Nuxalk Nation, said on Tuesday: “Our thoughts are with the victim’s family as they learn of this tragic event.” Schooner said a trapping effort to find the bear was under way and asked media to refrain from contacting community members.
The province’s premier-designate, Lorne Doerkson, called the news “heartbreaking” and said he was thinking of the victims’ family and the Nuxalk Nation.
“At a time of such profound grief and uncertainty, my thoughts are with everyone who is hurting and with all those supporting one another through an incredibly difficult day.”

articles.title_orig: Death toll hits 40 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site, dozens remain missing
articles.title_zh: Death toll hits 40 after Russian strike on Ukrainian aid site, dozens remain missing
articles.content_orig:
The death toll from a Russian bombing of an aid distribution point in Ukraine’s southeastern Zaporizhzhia region on Monday has risen to 40, ⁠with dozens still missing, officials said, in one of the deadliest strikes on civilians this year.
The attack came a day after a brief U.S.-brokered local ceasefire expired and less than a week before the United States is due to bring together Ukrainian and Russian delegations in Abu Dhabi for talks on ending the war , now in its fifth year.
Reuters footage on Wednesday showed men in military fatigues loading bodies in white plastic bags into the back of a ⁠van in the village of Komyshuvakha, which was struck multiple times.
Excavators were ​digging ⁠up earth near a huge blast crater while rescue workers searched underground for bodies.
Ivan Fedorov, the co-head of the Zaporizhzhia Regional Defense Council, wrote on Telegram that 59 people were missing.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Russian forces first dropped aerial ⁠bombs on an underground school building being used as a distribution point as people arrived to collect aid, then struck the ​shelter with ⁠more bombs.
Classes have long since been suspended at the ‌school because of its proximity to the front — Komyshuvakha lies some 11 miles from the nearest Russian positions — but it served as a shelter and handed out humanitarian aid every Monday, Zelenskyy said.
Two members of a rescue crew and four police officers were among the ‌dead, emergency services said.
Russia’s defense ministry said the attack targeted Ukrainian military units around ‌Komyshuvakha and two other settlements, and that up to 25 Ukrainian servicemen were killed.
Russia and Ukraine both deny deliberately targeting civilians.
Bodycam footage from one of the policemen killed in the attack, which Ukrainian police posted and Reuters verified, shows rubble and badly damaged buildings in the aftermath of the initial aerial attacks.
The policeman said the area was ⁠under threat from drones and appears to take shelter briefly inside the shell of a bombed-out building.
Later in the footage, 15 to 20 people in civilian clothing are gathered outside the entrance to an underground shelter when a warning comes over a radio that Russian glide bombs are heading in the direction of the village.
Residents rush down several flights of stairs and towards a room, while the policeman with the bodycam turns through a door into what appears to be a temporary police station.
Three other men and a woman are visible in the final frames before there is a large explosion and the camera turns black.
In a social media post accompanying the footage, the national police ‌said several strikes hit the area, including from a 3-ton FAB bomb, which is a large bomb fitted with ​a glide kit that allows it to fly long distances after being dropped from a Russian warplane.
According to defense intelligence ‌websites, a 3-ton glide bomb would carry around 1.4 tons of ⁠explosives.
The strike occurred a day after a six-day ceasefire to evacuate civilians from the ⁠Russian-occupied southern Ukrainian town of Oleshky expired.
The truce, brokered by first lady Melania Trump , allowed nearly 800 people to be evacuated, according to the first lady. Zelenskyy awarded Trump a state honour for her ​role.
The United States will bring together delegations from Ukraine and Russia in ‌Abu Dhabi on November 10 to 11 to discuss ending ​the conflict, postwar security agreements and de-escalation, US envoy Steve Witkoff said on Monday.

articles.title_orig: Trump can't pack the Fed board with allies now
articles.title_zh: Trump can't pack the Fed board with allies now
articles.content_orig:
Photo: The Federal Reserve Board of Governors in March 2026. Source: Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images.
Senate Democrats are likely to reject Fed nominees they view as insufficiently independent from the administration.
Trump has sought to replace Biden-appointed members of the Federal Reserve Board of Governors with allies, even before their terms expire. That effort now appears unlikely to succeed.
This is reported by Axios .
Trump is seeking to fire Governor Lisa Cook over alleged mortgage fraud. Courts have blocked the effort so far, and the White House plans a hearing on the allegations in December. Cook’s term runs through 2038.
Former Fed chair Jerome Powell remains a governor until January 2028. Michael Barr, appointed by Biden as the government’s top financial regulator, has a governor’s term through 2032. Philip Jefferson’s term as vice chair ends in September 2027, while his term as a governor runs through 2036.
If Trump fires Cook or removes any of the other three Biden-era holdovers on the seven-member board, a Democratic Senate will likely block replacements it considers insufficiently independent from the administration. Senator Elizabeth Warren is set to chair the Senate Banking Committee, which must advance Fed governor nominees. She has called chairman Kevin Warsh a “sock puppet” of the administration.
The governors staying in office until their terms end would break with recent precedent. In recent decades, Fed governor seats have turned over more regularly, particularly after a governor’s term as chair or vice chair ends. Powell, Barr and Jefferson may feel more comfortable leaving before their terms are up if they believe the Senate will block nominees who do not respect the tradition of central bank independence.
Only one Senate Democrat, John Fetterman, voted to confirm Warsh.

articles.title_orig: ‘Seismic shift’: World reacts to US midterm election results
articles.title_zh: ‘Seismic shift’: World reacts to US midterm election results
articles.content_orig:
Democrats in the United States have scored a major victory in midterm elections, taking control of both chambers of Congress in a stinging rebuke of President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.
The results are being carefully watched outside the US, as foreign leaders consider how the new political reality in Washington could affect US foreign policy – from the conflict with Iran to the Russia-Ukraine war and trade relations.
Trump himself has acknowledged the US-Israel war on Iran likely impacted his party’s poor performance in the elections, saying voters were probably not ready “for the short-term consequence of the price of gasoline”.
Here are the latest reactions from world leaders, as the scale of the Democratic victory continues to emerge:
European Parliament Vice President Christel Schaldemose said the US results left her “cautiously optimistic on Europe’s behalf”.
“Not because everything now ⁠⁠changes for the better, but because it could benefit the support for Ukraine, the green transition, and ⁠⁠relations with the rest of the world,” said Schaldemose in a post on X.
“But the EU must continue the course of standing stronger and standing on its own two feet. That’s not up for debate,” she added.
Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who is also the chief negotiator in talks with the US, said voters had rejected conflict.
“Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” wrote Ghalibaf in a post on X.
“If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare,” he added.
Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, meanwhile, said partisan shifts in Washington would not alter the US’s “hostility” towards Tehran.
“If there are still those who harbour even the slightest hope that the behaviour of the hegemonic system could change through party or factional shifts, or who believe that making concessions to the US could persuade it to abandon its hostility towards the Iranian people, they are gravely mistaken,” said Khamenei in a statement shared by Iranian state media.
There was no immediate reaction from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a Trump ally whose coalition lost its own majority in Israel’s parliament in elections last week.
However, opposition figure Yair Golan, whose party is in a coalition seeking to replace Netanyahu , said the US vote reveals “just how toxic Netanyahu has become” among US Democrats and Republicans alike.
He warned that if Netanyahu and his far-right government remain in power, Israel would be on “a path toward international sanctions, global isolation, and a confrontation with the United States – our most important friend and ally.”
Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid, also part of the anti-Netanyahu coalition, said the US vote effectively ruled out “any possibility of a unity government led by Netanyahu”.
German ⁠Chancellor Friedrich Merz suggested ⁠that, having lost control of Congress, Trump is likely to bypass it by using executive orders.
“Trump has, for ⁠the past ⁠two years, largely governed without consulting Congress,” Merz remarked. “Why should things ⁠be any ⁠different now?”
Berlin’s Defence Minister Boris Pistorius congratulated the Democratic Party on a “historic victory”, but reiterated that Europe must continue to raise its game regarding looking after its own security.
Health Minister James Frith stressed that the UK would maintain steady, strong ties with Washington despite an apparent “seismic shift in domestic politics for the Americans”.
“The change of emphasis of power in the States is frequent,” Frith told British media. “But the mainstay of the relationship with the UK Government, as its closest ally, is unwavering and unchanging.”
“So I don’t expect it to change the nature of the relationship at all; it remains very strong,” he added.
Finance Minister Roland Lescure said France would wait to see whether Trump, who remains in control of US foreign policy, adjusts his approach.
“Either he decides to rise above the fray – acknowledging that ‌‌changes are necessary, particularly regarding gasoline prices, which directly ‌‌affect people – and, I might add, he tones down his international involvement, or he does not,” Lescure told French TV. “Frankly, this is something we will need to keep an eye on in the ⁠⁠coming days.”
Left-wing Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said the US Democrats’ landslide victory was emblematic of the “unravelling” of the global far right.
“It happened in Brazil. It just happened in the US. And it will soon happen in Spain,” said Sanchez, whose own premiership is at stake in snap elections he called for November 29.
Sanchez said US voters had rejected policies that “only ‌‌impoverish”, as well as hate, sexism, climate change denialism and “the privileges of the elites”.
Government spokesman Pavlos Marinakis said US-Greek relations would not be affected by the election results.
“Greek-American relations will remain strong,” he told local media. “The United States is our strategic ally, and this will continue for major projects ⁠⁠and all major agreements. Nothing will be affected by this outcome. It is obvious that we respect every outcome. The conclusions are clear.”
Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov stressed the need to wait for the final results of US elections to come into focus, but noted that leaders in the US Democratic Party had a “sharply negative” approach to relations with Moscow.
Russia’s position on Ukraine and broader foreign policy “is not based on short-term considerations and, naturally, does not depend on the fluctuations of the political barometer in other countries,” Ryabkov was quoted by Russian state media as saying.
“We will continue our work in accordance with the directives of the President of the Russian Federation,” he added.
Kremlin spokesman ⁠Dmitry Peskov said Moscow hoped the US midterm results would not impact Trump’s “peacemaking efforts”.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Beijing would continue its “constructive strategic relationship” with the US, stressing that US elections are a “domestic affair”.
“China is willing to work with the US to safeguard and implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state, strengthen communication, properly manage differences and expand cooperation, build a constructive strategic relationship based on respect and equality,” Mao told reporters in Beijing.
Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said whatever the outcome of the US vote, “the Japan-US alliance is the cornerstone of Japan’s foreign and security policy”.
“As the international situation becomes turbulent and increasingly uncertain, a strong Japan-US alliance is essential for maximising Japan’s national interests and for peace and stability in the international community,” Kihara said at a press briefing.
⁠President Cyril Ramaphosa, who has clashed with Trump over the US president’s promotion of debunked claims of a white genocide in South Africa, said the election marks “a new era in world relations”.
“We have seen that the ⁠⁠Democrats have taken ⁠⁠control of the Senate and of ⁠⁠the House, and ⁠⁠the ⁠⁠people of America have spoken,” Ramaphosa told ‌‌reporters.
