articles.title_orig: CVS Health plans to split itself up. Here's why a breakup could make sense now
articles.title_zh: CVS Health plans to split itself up. Here's why a breakup could make sense now
articles.content_orig:
CVS Health plans to break itself up — and this time, the bet looks a lot more viable.
The healthcare conglomerate on Wednesday announced plans to split into two publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. CVS would separate its pharmacy business – including roughly 9,000 retail locations – from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark.
The move comes more than two years after CVS considered a breakup but ultimately walked away from the idea. At the time, analysts questioned whether the retail pharmacy business could survive on its own.
“Back then, the idea of retail standing alone was unthinkable,” Brian Tanquilut, senior equity research analyst at Jefferies, told CNBC.
But the economics of the businesses have changed: CVS's retail pharmacy business has become more consistently profitable, while its insurer, Aetna, has improved its performance despite persistently high medical costs in Medicare Advantage plans. That could make it easier for the company to separate the units — and for investors to recognize the value of each on its own, rather than valuing them together as one sprawling healthcare conglomerate.
“For us, it's showing the stability of the pharmacy,” Michael Cherny, senior research analyst at Leerink Partners, said in an interview. “This business is a much different business from the one that's been considered three years ago, five years ago, 10 years ago, where there had been a litany of headwinds that the pharmacy just couldn't overcome.”
CVS CEO David Joyner told CNBC’s "Squawk on the Street" on Wednesday that back in 2024, the company was "in a turnaround" without the flexibility, cash or business performance to execute a split. Now, CVS has posted eight consecutive quarters of beating Wall Street earnings estimates and has raised its guidance several times over the last two years, thanks to improvement across its PBM, pharmacy and insurer.
Since taking the helm in 2024, Joyner has pursued an aggressive turnaround plan that involves $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shakeups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs.
The company also now expects to generate at least $15.5 billion in operating cash flow in 2026, a roughly 70% increase from $9.1 billion in 2024, and says it has reached its leverage target ahead of schedule.
"What's changed in two years is the fact that we now can look at this business and the assets that are assembled and really determine, without any distress or without anything that we have to do, what is the right strategic decision to make," Joyner told analysts on a call Wednesday, adding that the decision comes "out of strength."
While investors have largely cheered CVS's progress in recent years, Wall Street appeared more pessimistic about Wednesday's announcement, as the company's shares dropped about 12%.
CVS's retail business has benefited from changes in the competitive landscape, including the widespread retrenchment and store closures of Walgreens, Rite Aid and other pharmacy operators over the last few years. That’s created opportunities for CVS to gain market share, some analysts told CNBC.
CVS has also introduced changes to its pharmacy reimbursement model. Its CostVantage program is designed to replace the traditional process with a more transparent, cost-based model. Some analysts say that has helped the company better align reimbursement with the cost of dispensing prescriptions and contributed to steadier profits.
Those developments represent a meaningful shift for a business that has faced years of pressure from declining prescription reimbursement, store closures and competition from online pharmacies and other retailers.
That doesn't mean the retail pharmacy has become a high-growth business. CVS's retail pharmacy segment remains a relatively low-margin operation, with adjusted operating margins of roughly 4% to 5%. But analysts say it may now be stable and profitable enough to operate independently – even if investors value it at a discount to CVS's other businesses.
In a note Wednesday, RBC Capital Markets analyst Ben Hendrix said the lower valuation investors assign to the retail pharmacy unit has weighed on CVS's overall value and obscured the earnings strength of businesses like Aetna and Caremark.
The underlying growth of the insurance and PBM businesses is also stronger than that of retail pharmacy, Tanquilut said, after accounting for changes to Caremark's rebate arrangements.
Aetna in particular has gotten a better handle on medical costs by exiting unprofitable markets, expanding value-based care models, and tightening utilization management.
The breakup also comes as Caremark faces mounting scrutiny over PBM practices, including state-level legal and regulatory challenges involving the businesses and their relationships with pharmacies.
Republicans in Tennessee and Arkansas have passed laws that would ban any one company from owning both a pharmacy and a PBM — thought the Arkansas measure has been held up in court. Cherny noted that legal hurdles involving PBMs in other states have continued to pile up.
“Through what seems to be a never-ending litany of state lawsuits, it feels like it's been under more pressure,” Cherny said. “It's unclear if it just became, for lack of a better term, too tenuous to move forward with those two entities combined as one. I’m not sure.”
Even so, Joyner told the Wall Street Journal that the company wasn’t splitting up because of regulatory issues. CVS has said the separation follows a strategic review and is intended to give each business greater focus and flexibility.
The move also marks a significant departure from the integrated healthcare strategy CVS spent years building.
CVS spent roughly $70 billion to acquire Aetna in 2018 and argued that combining health insurance, pharmacy benefit management, retail pharmacies and health providers under one roof would help coordinate care and create a competitive advantage. CVS was still promoting that model as recently as its investor day last year.
The proposed split suggests the company now sees more value in separating at least some of those businesses – though it is not abandoning vertical integration altogether.
Aetna and Caremark will remain together in the healthcare company, alongside CVS’s specialty pharmacy, its primary care clinic Oak Street Health and its home-visit provider Signify Health. The separate pharmacy company will include roughly 9,000 retail stores, mail pharmacy operations and MinuteClinic, a retail medical clinic located inside certain CVS locations.
Both sides are large enough that they can stand on their own, Cherny said. Caremark is one of the country's three largest PBMs, while CVS has one of the largest retail pharmacy footprints in the U.S.
But separating the company raises questions about how much of the commercial relationship between the businesses can survive.
The relationship has historically benefited both sides. As it stands, Caremark can use CVS's extensive retail footprint to offer members convenient access to prescriptions and steer them toward CVS locations through preferred pharmacy arrangements. Programs such as Maintenance Choice, for example, give eligible members the option to fill certain maintenance medications at CVS retail pharmacies or through mail order.
Those arrangements also helped direct prescription volume to CVS's stores, giving the retail pharmacy unit an important source of customers. Because the businesses shared a parent company, the financial benefits of that relationship ultimately went to CVS as a whole.
In a note, RBC's Hendrix also raised questions about how the split could impact Aetna's Medicare Advantage quality ratings, which determine whether health plans qualify for bonus payments from the government. Retail pharmacists have played a role in engaging Aetna members, and a separation could complicate that relationship.

articles.title_orig: Oil prices drop below $100 as midterms fuel hope for an end to the Iran war
articles.title_zh: Oil prices drop below $100 as midterms fuel hope for an end to the Iran war
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices dropped sharply Wednesday, propelled by growing hopes for a resolution in the Iran war.
European Brent crude fell below $100 per barrel for the first time since Oct. 7. The move translated to a nearly $8 drop, or an 8.3% decline. U.S. crude oil, or West Texas Intermediate, also slipped 8.3% to close at about $88.12. It was oil’s biggest daily decline since April.
Relief for consumers may follow. Oil’s fall could bring the national average price of gas down below $4 in the “days ahead,” Patrick De Haan, an analyst at GasBuddy, said.
Prices moved lower as trading desks and energy experts watched closely for a sign that Tuesday’s midterm election results would pressure President Donald Trump into ending the Iran war without a major escalation. The war sent gasoline and diesel prices skyrocketing, making already stubborn inflation worse for American consumers, farmers and business owners.
“The next six weeks typically deliver one of the most hostile environments for higher gasoline and diesel prices,” Tom Kloza, chief energy adviser to Gulf Oil, said on social media. “If the US or Iran don’t pursue ‘scorched earth’ policies in the Persian Gulf, we may see considerably lower prices by second half December.”
On Wednesday morning, that average price was $4.12 . That’s 39% higher than before Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu launched the Iran war Feb. 28, which snarled shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz.
On social media , Vice President JD Vance said the war is the reason the Republican Party suffered such steep losses in the midterm elections.
“And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” said Vance, who could be the GOP’s standard-bearer in the 2028 presidential election.
Trump also said he realized the toll the Iran war took on American consumers.
“I think it’s the gasoline price,” Trump said Tuesday night on Fox News as the first results became clear. “People agree with what I’m doing on Iran, but they really probably weren’t willing to do the short-term consequence of paying more for gasoline, and that, you know, I understand that.”
Oil’s drop over the last three trading sessions has been precipitous. On Friday, Brent oil traded as high as $118 per barrel, but by Wednesday, its price was around $94.
Despite the sharp move lower, the overall price of oil remains higher by 60% compared with the start of the year.
On Tuesday, 59% of voters who went to the ballot box told NBC News in an exit poll that they were “very concerned” with the cost of gas and diesel fuel, echoing concerns that consumers have voiced for months.
But diesel fuel prices have economists far more concerned.
U.S. diesel futures also tumbled Wednesday. As of midday, prices declined by nearly 7%, to their lowest level since the end of August. That likely means that more relief is coming for prices at the pump.
As the fuel that powers transportation services for goods, such as groceries, across the country, any jump in prices could quickly ripple across the economy through higher prices on store shelves.
Steve Kopack is a senior reporter at NBC News covering business and the economy.

articles.title_orig: Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign gets new update from leaker
articles.title_zh: Next year’s iPhone Pro redesign gets new update from leaker
articles.content_orig:
Apple reportedly has a big redesign coming to next year’s iPhone Pro models, timed for the iPhone’s 20th anniversary. The latest leak about the design reveals that the dream of a cutout-free display may remain a dream for now.
Yesterday Weibo leaker Digital Chat Station outlined three new iPhone models coming in early 2027: iPhone 18e, iPhone 18, and iPhone Air 2.
His main focus was on the iPhone 18, which is expected to get two Pro-inspired upgrades .
In a follow-up post though, replying to another Weibo user’s question, the leaker addressed a key design question regarding next fall’s iPhone Pro models.
Apple is rumored to be working on a big redesign timed for the iPhone’s 20th anniversary. It will reportedly feature a quad-curved display that wraps around the edges of the device for a visually bezel-free look.
Early rumors indicated the device could also drop the Dynamic Island for a truly all-glass display, with no cutouts.
But according to Digital Chat Station, that’s not happening after all.
After being asked if the ‘iPhone 20 Pro Max’ will have a Dynamic Island still, or feature a hole-free display, the leaker confirmed the display will still have holes . Thus, it will retain the Dynamic Island cutout.
It’s unclear if the Dynamic Island will be the same size as that of iPhone 18 Pro, but since the device is expected to have Face ID, that’s highly likely.
Does the inclusion of a display cutout change your interest in the iPhone 20 Pro at all? Let us know in the comments.

articles.title_orig: From Iran to trade: how the US midterms impact the rest of the world
articles.title_zh: From Iran to trade: how the US midterms impact the rest of the world
articles.content_orig:
A display shows currency exchange information in Tehran, Iran, September 27, 2026
Photo by Majid Asgaripour/West Asia News Agency via Reuters
By Raphael S. Cohen and Howard J. Shatz
This commentary was originally published by Foreign Policy on October 26, 2026.
So far, the Iran war has cost the United States 800 casualties, tens of billions of dollars, hundreds of damaged or destroyed buildings on U.S. military bases in the region, and a drawdown of munitions that is straining supplies. Fuel prices have risen sharply since the start of the war, pushing U.S. inflation to a level last seen in 2023. According to polls, most Americans do not believe there was “sufficient reason” for the United States to attack Iran, and public opposition to the war has increased over time. And there is little sign that the fighting is coming to a close. As of now, the Iranian regime seems disinclined to cease its attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, stop its regional proxies from attacking elsewhere, or curb its nuclear program.
What should the United States do now?
In broad strokes, there are three options. First, ramp the war back up. Some—including U.S. President Donald Trump—have floated the idea of returning to a full-scale bombing campaign similar to what we saw during the conflict's initial phase. Others have proposed escalating the war , for example by using ground forces to seize Iranian territory.
At the other end of the spectrum lies a second option: The United States could walk away from the conflict. Even Republican supporters of the Trump administration have increasingly called for an end to the war.
The third option is to stay the current course: Maintain the blockade and economic pressure campaign, respond with force when Iran or its proxies strike U.S. or partner targets, and push for negotiations that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and end the Iranian nuclear program. Of the three options, this may be the least satisfying; it almost certainly will not bring quick results. But it is strategically prudent.
As messy as the conflict has been, the U.S. blockade of Iran and the wider Operation Economic Outcast are going in the direction that the United States wants.
As messy as the conflict has been, the U.S. blockade of Iran and the wider Operation Economic Outcast are going in the direction that the United States wants. Iran is imploding economically. Its currency recently traded at 2.5 million rials to the dollar, a dramatic depreciation from about 630,000 to the dollar in 2024. Inflation has recently reached almost 90 percent , with food inflation at almost 130 percent. Moreover, Iran's floating oil storage—a shadow fleet of tankers anchored outside the Strait of Hormuz, whose cargo has mitigated some of the effects of the blockade—is now depleted. That further increases the pressure on the Iranian economy.
Although the U.S. spot price has risen above $100 per barrel at times, oil is still priced well below previous peaks once you adjust for inflation . Middle Eastern crude is also again flowing out of the region at near prewar levels, although other critical commodities—liquefied natural gas, refined fuels, fertilizer—remain bottlenecked.
To be fair, economic coercion—even when it causes a full economic crisis—has a mixed track record in effecting regime change. Major economic dislocations have sometimes led to dramatic changes in government, as in Yugoslavia following years of economic problems in the 1980s. Inflationary crises can facilitate democratization , as happened in much of Latin America in the 1980s. But in other cases, such as the U.S. pressure campaigns against Cuba and North Korea, the regimes were still able to use what resources they had to maintain their hold on power.
The history of the last Iran nuclear deal shows that economic pressure campaigns have a better record when they are aimed at achieving more modest objectives. In that case, mounting economic duress forced even the Iranian regime's hard-liners to the negotiating table. This time around, the regime seems even less inclined to make concessions, at least judging from its public statements, but the pressure campaign is also more extreme.
The primary downside to maintaining the current approach is that it is unlikely to lead to a swift resolution of the conflict.
The primary downside to maintaining the current approach is that it is unlikely to lead to a swift resolution of the conflict. Strategies built around economic pressure generally take months or even years to succeed. But time is on Washington's side. The blockade is continuing to bite under economic conditions that some deem “unbearable,” with unemployment rising and this year's GDP projected to shrink by 7.6 percent . If Iran can stabilize its economy, the United States will need to alter its approach. But if not, the Iranian regime—as fractured and hard-line as it may be—will sooner or later need to compromise to avoid collapse.
Moreover, the alternatives to staying the course are worse. Resuming a full-scale war to “blow the entire nation up” is unlikely to be feasible. Even if we bracket concerns over U.S. weapons stockpiles, air campaigns alone have rarely succeeded in overthrowing a government. Plus, given the intensity of the bombardment in the opening weeks of the war, it's hard to imagine what more the United States could do from the air that would tip the balance. Removing the Iranian regime by ground power would be a Herculean undertaking: Compared with Iraq, the site of the last major U.S. war in the region, Iran has nearly double the population and almost quadruple the territory.
Returning to large-scale conflict would also come at a cost. Despite the effectiveness of the bombardment from February to April, Iran still has the ability to produce missiles and drones. U.S. military casualties stand at 15 killed and more than 800 wounded , a figure that would almost certainly rise if the conflict intensified. Similarly, the war has already taken a toll on military equipment and bases in the region, and more damage would be incurred if the conflict flares up again. Then there are the less tangible costs, such as the erosion of Washington's global reputation, especially if military strikes hit civilian infrastructure.
Then there is the global economic cost of a renewed large-scale conflict. Analysts estimate that it could take years to fully repair the damage to the Middle East's energy infrastructure that has occurred so far. A return to hostilities would risk further damage to these already battered facilities, not to mention the prospect of even higher energy prices.
More modest military options also come with significant risks. The most widely discussed option is the seizure of Kharg Island , an island around 20 miles off the Iranian coast that serves as the country's hub for 90 percent of its oil exports. This would aim to either destabilize the regime or use the island as a bargaining chip in future negotiations. Although the United States certainly has the capacity to seize the island, the challenge would be holding the territory afterward. The island is well within range of Iranian missiles and drones , leaving any troops stationed there and resupply efforts vulnerable to attack. Air defenses provide only a partial solution, so the United States would likely sustain casualties. This would also create political pressure on the United States to abandon the island prematurely—before it could pressure Iran into a lasting settlement.
Walking away from the war would carry its own costs.
Walking away from the war, by contrast, carries its own costs. Iran has so far rejected proposals to allow the free passage of global exports through Hormuz in exchange for an end to the blockade. Unilaterally dropping the blockade would effectively leave the Strait of Hormuz in Iranian hands, allowing the regime to tax transiting ships as it sees fit. articles.title_orig: America’s grid upgrade hinges on a 400-ton machine designed in the 1800s
articles.title_zh: America’s grid upgrade hinges on a 400-ton machine designed in the 1800s
articles.content_orig:
Americans have a lot of plans for the country’s power grid. Some people want to expand renewable energy by building solar and wind farms . Others want to add new coal- or natural gas-fired power plants . There are those who want to provide power to some unknown number of data centers processing artificial intelligence algorithms.
To accomplish any of these goals, the country will need a significant number of pieces of equipment whose design was invented in the late 19th century: large power transformers . These giant metal structures are about the size of a two-story house and weigh as much as 400 tons – roughly equivalent to a fully loaded Boeing 747 . They convert high voltages used to transmit electricity down to voltage levels people can use in their homes and businesses. And they are made largely in the same way they were when they were invented 150 years ago .
Many of the large power transformers in service in the U.S. and around the world are aging beyond their intended lifespans . And there aren’t enough replacements to meet the world’s needs. It can take more than three years for a company’s order to be filled and delivered.
Large power transformers are crucial to transporting electricity over long distances . Power plants – whether coal- or gas-fired, hydropower dams, or solar or wind farms – are often far from the customers who need the electricity that’s generated.
Transmitting power through wires generates heat , which over a long distance dramatically reduces the amount of energy arriving at the far end. To reduce energy losses, power companies use large transformers to increase the voltage. You can think of this like freight being loaded onto large trucks and directed over interstate highways. They can carry a lot of energy more efficiently than smaller cars could on smaller roads.
But the high-voltage power is not safe for a home or business to use right away, just as a semitruck at highway speeds shouldn’t try to enter your driveway. So when the power arrives near a group of customers, it needs to take an off-ramp, going through another large transformer that lowers its voltage to levels regular customers can use. Then low-voltage lines act as local city streets, delivering the electricity the short distance from the highway exit to homes and businesses.
Between 2019 and 2025, demand for generator step-up transformers, those that connect power plants to the transmission grid, nearly tripled . And over the same period, demand for transformers to work as off-ramps more than doubled, with costs increasing 80% .
These devices are not mass-produced from automated assembly lines. They are custom-engineered to meet specific needs and demands for their intended destinations. If a specialized transformer fails during an extreme storm or heat wave, there aren’t just replacements waiting in a warehouse somewhere.
What these transformers are made of is a big part of the delay.
One key ingredient is what’s known as grain-oriented electrical steel . This is not at all average steel. It is manufactured using precise thermal and mechanical processes that position the steel’s magnetic crystals in a single direction. The crystalline alignment allows magnetic fields to pass through the metal with low energy loss, which is crucial for handling large amounts of electricity. However, only a handful of specialized steel mills worldwide have the technology to produce it. Just one mill is in the U.S.
Also in short supply is copper , which is made into wires that are wrapped around the core of the transformer , typically made of steel, to achieve the correct voltage adjustment.
Because of the transformer shortage, it can take utilities and power producers more than two years to get equipment to connect new power plants to the grid – regardless of whether they are powered by nuclear energy, fossil fuels, solar energy or the wind.
To get around that delay, companies that run data centers to power artificial intelligence systems have sought to bypass the grid altogether, by installing  dedicated, on-site natural gas power plants to run the computer centers.
That move has caused another supply chain problem . Gas turbines burn at over 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit (1,100 C), which is hot enough to melt standard steel. Turbine blades are manufactured with a complicated process out of very specialized combinations of metal and coated with ceramic heat shields .
As tech companies have placed more and larger orders, the time between ordering a gas turbine and having it delivered has stretched to between three and seven years . And prices in 2027 are expected to be nearly triple what they were in 2019 , due to the increase in demand and still-rare materials.
A supply chain built in the 19th century is struggling to reliably serve power to the 21st-century economy.
Large power transformers are also key to upgrading the existing grid and reducing its vulnerability to large storms or extended outages .
The solutions are both concrete and complicated.
The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency has recommended standardizing transformer designs , rather than having each be custom-built. That would allow manufacturers to produce more units more quickly, with an assembly line-style process. It would also allow utility companies to share emergency spares.
The U.S. Department of Energy has recommended deploying what are collectively called “ grid-enhancing technologies .” These methods include sensors that monitor in real time exactly how much power can be transmitted through long-distance wires and advanced software that can find alternative routes by which to distribute electricity from power plants to maximize what’s available to customers. Together, these types of systems can allow the transmission of 15% to 20% more electricity than without them, easing bottlenecks while waiting for new transformers to be delivered.
Longer term, the U.S. could produce more grain-oriented electrical steel, process more copper and expand its capacity to build large power transformers.
All the ways people want to adapt, improve, expand and modernize the power grid are dependent on this one type of equipment. Without large power transformers, none of the efforts will get very far.
In a sense, leaders face a choice either way: solve these hardware shortages or accept the default consequences of grid congestion, delayed projects and rising costs. Resolving the transformer bottleneck would be what turns that passive reality into active choice.
Jasmine Garland , Chancellors Postdoctoral Fellow in Civil, Environmental and Architectural Engineering, University of Colorado Boulder

articles.title_orig: Trump's midterm drubbing demonstrates the power of data center opponents
articles.title_zh: Trump's midterm drubbing demonstrates the power of data center opponents
articles.content_orig:
China, Canada, India and South Africa could gain fresh leverage in trade negotiations with Washington after Democrats seized control of both chambers of the US Congress, weakening President Donald Trump's political position amid growing discontent over the Iran war, rising consumer prices and his controversial trade tariffs.
The November 3 midterm elections saw Republicans lose their majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives, with Democrats securing victories in Republican strongholds, including Texas, Kansas and South Carolina.
Republicans suffered the setback amid rising living costs, Trump's tariffs and the eight-month Iran war, which disrupted energy supplies and pushed Brent crude to $138.21 per barrel in April, its highest level since 2008, fuelling US inflation.
From what Business Insider Africa has gathered, the results could encourage America's trade rivals and dissatisfied partners to resist Washington's demands, delay investments and seek better trade deals as Trump will now have to answer to a Democrat-controlled Congress.
DON'T MISS: Despite warnings from China, Saudi Arabia and Turkey, Israel presses ahead with embassy plans in breakaway African territory near Red Sea
China is among the countries that could use Trump's weakened political position to push for more favourable trade terms, particularly as Beijing seeks to recover exports lost to American tariffs.
The impact of those restrictions is reflected in US trade figures, which show that America's goods trade deficit with China narrowed from $295.5 billion in 2024 to $202.1 billion in 2025.
With a temporary trade truce approaching expiration in January 2027, Beijing could seek lower tariffs and fewer technology restrictions, calculating that Trump faces greater political resistance to another trade war.
Saul Eslake, an economist at Corinna Economic Advisory in Australia, believes China could take advantage of the changing political balance in Washington.
"Xi Jinping will recognize that Trump's authority has been greatly weakened by these results, and will no doubt be thinking about ways of exploiting that," Eslake told Reuters.
Although Beijing has not publicly indicated plans to exploit Trump's political setback, China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning described the elections as an internal US matter, saying the country would continue managing differences and expanding cooperation with Washington.
DON'T MISS: Two Chinese mining firms pull out of Kenya’s rare earth and niobium extraction race as three American companies stand their ground among five remaining bidders
Canada could also find greater support in Washington after months of difficult trade negotiations between Prime Minister Mark Carney and Trump's administration over tariffs and market access.
Talks stalled in August after Ottawa rejected American demands, while tariffs on Canadian steel, aluminium and other products continued to strain relations between the neighbouring economies.
In an October 30 interview with POLITICO, Carney indicated that Canada would rather wait for another American president than accept an unfavourable agreement.
Asked whether Canada could hold out until Trump's successor took office, he replied: "Well, if that's what it takes, yeah."
His position could receive support from Democrats, particularly Senator Ron Wyden, a senior member of the Senate Finance Committee, who has called for removing tariffs on Canadian goods because of their impact on businesses and consumers.
DON'T MISS: European nation stops foreign workers and students from South Africa, Ghana, India and other countries from applying for residence permits inside the country
India could gain negotiating flexibility as New Delhi seeks better trade terms while American consumers face higher prices on imported goods.
Washington imposed tariffs of up to 50% on Indian products in 2025 amid trade disputes and disagreements over India's purchases of Russian oil. The restrictions affected textiles, jewellery and footwear, increasing costs for American importers.
The countries agreed in February 2026 to a framework reducing tariffs on most Indian goods to 18%, but negotiations remain unfinished.
Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said the agreement had reached the final drafting stage, although New Delhi would proceed only if it secured an advantage over competing exporters.
Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman also acknowledged in October that further concessions would be "very, very difficult" for both sides.
The Democratic victory could encourage India to resist additional demands as Trump faces greater scrutiny of his trade policies from the Democrat-controlled Congress.
South Africa faces a trade setback after Washington announced on November 2 that it would remove the country from the African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) on January 1, 2027, following months of diplomatic tensions over Pretoria's domestic and foreign policies.
The decision threatens preferential access for South African exports, including vehicles, citrus fruits and wine, adding to existing trade pressures after the country's agricultural exports to the US fell by 28% in the second quarter of 2026.
President Cyril Ramaphosa previously urged South Africans to prepare for possible exclusion, saying: "We should not go out and jump off tall buildings and think that this is the end of the world."
However, in a sharp reversal of his earlier cautious stance, Ramaphosa welcomed the Democratic victory on November 4, saying: "We have seen that the Democrats have taken control of the Senate and of the House, and the people of America have spoken."
He added that the results could introduce "a new era in world relations", raising hopes of improved ties with Washington.
"We're hoping that, on a bilateral basis, there will be a coming together of minds, where we will find a proper path forward on geopolitics as well as on trade matters and investment matters," Ramaphosa said.

articles.title_orig: UK Supreme Court hears appeal against Palestine Action’s proscription
articles.title_zh: UK Supreme Court hears appeal against Palestine Action’s proscription
articles.content_orig:
An appeal challenging the designation of Palestine Action as a “terrorist” organisation has begun at the United Kingdom’s top court, as police arrested demonstrators who gathered outside to protest against the group’s proscription.
The two-day hearing at the Supreme Court in London began on Wednesday. Huda Ammori, cofounder of Palestine Action, said ahead of the hearing that she would argue the ban is having a disproportionate effect on freedom of speech and the right to protest.
The direct action group was proscribed by the UK government under then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer in July last year. The decision has since been denounced by rights groups, including Amnesty International and Liberty.
Palestine Action describes itself as a “direct action movement committed to ending global participation in Israel’s genocidal and apartheid regime”. Its designation as a “terrorist” organisation puts it on the same list as armed groups such as al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS). Those found guilty of belonging to or supporting Palestine Action could face up to 14 years in prison.
As the hearing got under way, protesters gathered outside the court. Some expressed support for Palestine Action, while others opposed the group’s proscription, which many view as an affront to civil liberties. One demonstrator held a placard reading: “God help us Jews who support Palestine and Palestine Action”.
About 25 protesters were arrested, according to the Press Association; the final person detained carried a sign saying: “God help us who are not married to the UK’s national security adviser who support Palestine and Palestine action.”
It’s understood that this is in reference to journalist and author Sarah Helm, who is married to the UK prime minister’s national security adviser, and who had earlier posted a similar line on X but did not face prosecution.
In a statement issued after the first day of the hearing, Ammori said that “overwhelming evidence” given to the court by United Nations experts, Amnesty International, Liberty and the former director of MI6 showed that the “dangerous and disproportionate proscription” had criminalised legitimate protest as “terrorism” for the “first time in British history”.
She said the government’s submissions were “particularly lacklustre”.
Ammori said the government was “clearly struggling with the consequences of this ban”.
Ammori said Palestine Action “has never advocated violence against any person”, and that it used tactics including “graffiti, petty vandalism, occupation and lock-ons”.
More than 4,000 people had been arrested for peacefully opposing Israel’s war on Gaza, she noted.
“This ban has made Britain an international aberration on free speech.” Ammori urged the justices “to bring this authoritarian overreach… to an end once and for all”.
“Today was another demonstration of the chaos wrought by the Government’s grave misuse of terrorism powers to proscribe Palestine Action,” Tom Southerden, Amnesty International’s UK Law and Human Rights director, said in a statement issued after Wednesday’s arrests.
“The sight of musicians, politicians and celebrities being arrested for peacefully holding placards is a grim one. That they were arrested for using the same language that Sarah Helm didn’t face arrest for, shows how dangerously vague our terrorism laws are.”
Amnesty is one of several organisations calling for the UK government to lift the ban on Palestine Action.
“Whatever the Supreme Court ultimately decides, it’s long past time for the Government to admit they got this badly wrong, end the proscription of Palestine Action and put a stop to these appalling arrests,” Southerden said.
The UK government’s crackdown on pro-Palestine voices has come under intense scrutiny since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza more than three years ago.
Last week, Swedish academic Andreas Malm was prevented from entering the UK after the government said his presence was “not conducive to the public good”. Malm is a vocal supporter of Palestine and has spoken out against Israel’s assault on Gaza.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said before taking office in July that the Labour Party had “got it wrong” on Gaza. However, his comments have come under renewed scrutiny after Malm was refused entry to the UK last week.

articles.title_orig: Ukrainian Soldiers Tell Us Which Guns And Optics Work Best In Combat
articles.title_zh: Ukrainian Soldiers Tell Us Which Guns And Optics Work Best In Combat
articles.content_orig:
When it comes to what rifles, sidearms and optics work best in war, there is perhaps no better place to find out than Ukraine. During more than four years of intense defense of their homeland , Ukrainian troops have used an assortment of small arms and accessories, many foreign-made, others domestically produced, to fight the Russians.
To get a better sense of what Ukrainians are currently using on the front lines, what they like, and what they don’t, we reached out to the First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine. The unit is stationed in the bloody Dobropillia sector in the eastern Donetsk region and is in the middle of one of the toughest fights in Ukraine.
Five soldiers from different Azov units with a range of specialties offered their unique insights into the weapons, sights and scopes they like and the ones they don’t.
The soldiers are issued all their weapons exclusively through the brigade’s armament service, which obtains them from the Ukrainian Defense Ministry (MoD). Individuals, however, told us they sometimes purchase their own sights and scopes and other accessories, depending on the models.
Some of the questions and answers have been slightly edited for clarity.
Tarantino, Chief Armorer, 12th Special Forces Brigade Azov, First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine.
When it comes to light weapon systems, the most common is an assault rifle based on the AR-15 [chambered 5.56mm], either domestic production or the one given to us by partner countries.
Chill, Chief Tactical Training Instructor, 41st Unmanned Systems Regiment Pilum, First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine .
So, in my personal opinion, the UAR-15 system is better for me because it’s lighter and it’s more reliable. I have worked with both platforms, both systems, and I can compare them based on my experience. And from my personal experience, the AR system is better.
The caliber is 5.56, and it’s also really convenient in terms of its modification and modernization because with the AK platform, you need to adapt it for further adjustments individually. But in the case of the UAR system, it’s really adaptable and you do not basically need anything in order to modernize it or modify it.
Khalepa, Anti-Aircraft Artillery Battery Commander, Air Defense Battalion Strazh, First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine.
Well, in our case, we are using larger calibers starting from 12.7mm up to 35mm. So we do not actually use the standard rifles.
Chewie, Deputy Commander for Logistics, Separate Special Operations Detachment Tuman, First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine.
When it comes to close combat, usually this is the UAR-15S of Ukrainian manufacturer called Zbroyar.
Barman, Tactical Training Instructor, Personnel Training Battalion, First Corps Azov of the National Guard of Ukraine.
So currently our key weapon platform is the UAR-15, but previously we also used the AK-74 and other modifications. The AK-74 fires 5.45mm rounds.
Well, the best weapon to work with is not the weapon itself, but the people we are working with. The weapon is only the instrument. But personally, the most reliable weapon is the one that has as few stoppages as possible because the last thing you want is to have a stoppage in the situation where you need to fire.
For me, that is the Heckler & Koch 416 . But I am talking about my preferences and experience. That gun has a gas piston system that has proven itself the most efficient due to the fact that the movement of the piston back and forth is relatively short. That makes the weapon itself much more reliable.
Another system, called DI [ direct impingement used in standard AR-15 pattern rifles], requires much more attention from the gunner who is shooting the rifle. Because in the conditions where the operator, the marksman, is sitting in the trench or in a bunker — especially now in autumn when the humidity is high — this DI system requires much more attention due to the wet weather around. The gas piston system has proven itself much more reliable and it doesn’t need that much attention.
We are using the Ukrainian-manufactured UAR-15 rifle, and you know, as they say, the best rifle is the one that you have.
So the weapon system that I told you about, UAR-15, is indeed the most loved because, in addition to this weapon, we do possess small numbers of Beretta, Bren, and several other weapon systems.
The reason why we prefer the UAR-15 is, first of all, it is much lighter. Second, it’s shorter. Another reason is that, taking into account the combat warfare that we have right now, we have the manufacturer on the premises of our country. It means if something happens to the weapon, it doesn’t take much time to either send the request to the manufacturer for them to send us the spare details, or for us to send the weapon system to them for maintenance.
Our preference is of course the UAR-15, and we’re using the 5.56 UAR platforms because it’s more convenient to use, it’s easier to maintain, and it’s also more reliable. But we also need to understand that our enemy is using the AK platforms, the AK-12 , the AK-74, and while of course we are carrying the 5.56 rounds, usually during the assault actions, we can take the AK rifles and the 5.45 rounds to be able to use our rifles in compatibly with the enemy’s rifles. We can use the AKs for the element of surprise and for deception. The way they look compared to the UAR rifles makes it easier to deceive the enemy.
Well, again, the biggest difference between this gas piston system and the DI system is that the gas piston system has a very short movement back and forth of the piston. It means that the chances of stoppage in this weapon are quite low, while the DI system is much more demanding because these exhaust gases go back into this tube that pushes the bolt carrier back. That means these gases make this tunnel much more dirty. And in a situation when the rotation of the soldier to the battlefield is for two weeks, and these are the two weeks of a very intensive fight, a soldier doesn’t always have the chance to disassemble a weapon and pull the bolt carrier out and clean it.
Compared to the DI system, the Heckler & Koch quality of the barrel itself is exceptionally phenomenal. So the quality of the metal is good, and it allows you to shoot even four or five or even six magazines in a row without the barrel getting overheated.
Well, talking about the piston system, the only AR-15-based rifle which I know has the piston system is the Heckler & Koch 416. So I have some experience in using it, but unfortunately I do not have this rifle. But I would like to. It’s quite reliable based on my communication with other operators and service members. I also get really good feedback about that weapon. But that’s the only weapon system with this piston system that I know of, and yeah, it presents some advantages.
The UAR-15 system that we are currently using within our unit is the DI-based weapon system, and the key difference is that they become contaminated quicker, and they require better and more frequent maintenance, which is not always possible to ensure in combat conditions.
Well, I have served in the infantry since 2022, and I have had some experience with the piston systems, for instance, with the AK system, and I did not really notice any major differences.
We use only the DI system.
Well, from my experience, the gas piston systems like the one that we can find on the HK 416 , they are simpler to maintain. They are more efficient in terms of their principle of operation, and also they are more reliable, I would say.
But the key difference in the DI system is that, of course, it’s a little bit more difficult to maintain them. But at the same time, you can regulate the amount of gas that goes back into the receiver. So, both of these systems have their own advantages and disadvantages.
If I were asked to choose between the two, I would use the gas piston system. It also has fewer

articles.title_orig: Bukele warns Haitian gang leaders that his forces will 'finish' them as he did in El Salvador
articles.title_zh: Bukele warns Haitian gang leaders that his forces will 'finish' them as he did in El Salvador
articles.content_orig:
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele says his troops will rescue four missing technicians by force if Haitian gangs refuse to hand them over. (Reuters.)
After crushing powerful criminal gangs in El Salvador, President Nayib Bukele has turned his attention to the Caribbean nation of Haiti, deploying 2,000 troops after four Salvadoran military aviation technicians disappeared following an Oct.18 ambush near Port-au-Prince.
"We have already finished with the gangs in El Salvador, and we can finish with you too," Bukele wrote in a message on X directed at Haiti's criminal groups. Bukele stressed that the operation's objective was not to invade Haiti or conduct a long-term occupation, but to recover the four missing Salvadorans alive.
The disappearance has become a national priority for Bukele, who has warned Haitian gang leaders that El Salvador is prepared to use overwhelming force if the men are not returned alive.
FLORIDA JURY CONVICTS 4 MEN WHO PLOTTED ASSASSINATION OF HAITI'S PRESIDENT FROM SOUTH FLORIDA HUB
In a screen grab taken from a video released Oct. 29, 2026, soldiers walk across the airport tarmac to board an aircraft after El Salvador's deployment of thousands of troops to Haiti, days after four Salvadoran members of a U.N.-backed force went missing in a gang ambush, in Comalapa, El Salvador. (Handout via Reuters)
The aviation technicians were assigned to a medical unit as part of the United Nations -backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) in Haiti when their armored vehicle was attacked in Croix-des-Bouquets. Haiti’s National Police announced Tuesday, more than two weeks after the attack, that it had found the charred remains of the vehicle in the Santo neighborhood of Croix-des-Bouquets. Police said, however, they found no sign of the missing men.
El Salvador says the men were abducted, the Haitian government says the soldiers are missing, and one gang leader says they are dead.
In a post on X Tuesday, directed at the "Haitian people" and written in Haitian creole, Bukele recalled the 1806 assassination of Jean-Jacques Dessalines, who proclaimed Haiti’s independence from France in 1804 and who many regard as the founder of Haiti.
"Dessalines liberated Haiti, but some people who were by his side betrayed him and killed him," Bukele said. "Those traitors still exist in Haiti."
SUSPECTS IN HAITIAN PRESIDENT'S ASSASSINATION TRANSFERRED TO MIAMI, ACCUSED OF FUNDING PLOT WITH COVID FRAUD
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele joined the annual National Prayer Breakfast in Washington, D.C., warning attendees that violent gang members in his country have a documented history of worshiping Satan. (Alex Pena/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Bukele also reposted video of a helicopter engagement in Croix-des-Bouquets.
"Gangs were attacking GSF soldiers from Chad," he wrote. "We arrived quickly and repelled the attackers with our attack helicopters."
Bukele has the backing of President Donald Trump, who, when asked by reporters at Mar-a-Lago on Halloween, confirmed speaking with the Salvadoran president.
"He said that he has a big problem with Haiti," Trump said. "They killed some of his people. I said, 'You're running your country. You have to do what you have to do.'"
Unlike previous foreign interventions, Bukele's deployment has the backing of Haiti's transitional government.
"The international force is not here to replace the state," Haitian Prime Minister Didier Fils-Aimé said Tuesday in his first remarks about the deployment. "They're here to support us."
Fils-Aimé added that Bukele "understands our fight. … He came to stand on the side of the Haitian people."
‘DONROE’ DOCTRINE AND CONSERVATIVE VICTORIES SQUEEZE CARTELS IN LATIN AMERICA
An armored personnel carrier of Haiti's U.N.-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) patrols an area after El Salvador announced a rescue mission for four air force members in the GSF who went missing after a gang ambush in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Oct. 23, 2026. (Patrice Noel/Reuters)
The operation has drawn criticism from human-rights advocates and gang leaders who warn that a military escalation could worsen civilian suffering. The U.N. says at least 5,700 people have been killed or injured due to the gang violence in Haiti since Jan. 1 as security forces struggle to contain the violence.
The U.N. has also indicated that El Salvador’s deployment is separate from the GSF and has warned El Salvador must follow applicable international law.
One of those gang leaders is Wilson Joseph, known as "Lanmò Sanjou," leader of the powerful 400 Mawozo gang. He accused rival gang Chen Mechan of carrying out the ambush and claimed the Salvadorans are dead, he told The Associated Press.
Joseph also sent a letter to United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres asking the U.N. for mediation and warning Bukele's "vengeful remarks, expectations, and threats … will lead to an escalation of violence and a logic of reprisals, of which the Haitian people would be the first victims."
EXCLUSIVE: HAITIAN ILLEGAL ALIEN GANG MEMBER WHO WENT VIRAL YELLING ‘BIDEN FOREVER’ DURING ICE ARREST DEPORTED
An armed member of the G9 and Family gang patrols a roadblock in the Delmas 6 neighborhood of Port-au-Prince, Haiti, March 11. (AP Photo/Odelyn Joseph)
Joseph was indicted by the U.S. in 2022 on hostage-taking charges related to the 2021 kidnapping of 17 missionaries, including 16 Americans, and remains the subject of a reward of up to $1 million for his arrest.
Bukele dismissed such appeals, accusing gang leaders of attempting to use civilians and international concerns about human rights as a shield to preserve their power and avoid accountability. Bukele has said that negotiations have only prolonged the crisis that has devastated Haiti for years.
After years as one of the world's most violent countries, dominated by powerful gangs including MS-13 , El Salvador launched an unprecedented crackdown in 2022 under a state of emergency. Authorities carried out tens of thousands of arrests, ultimately detaining more than 90,000 suspected gang members.
Supporters credit the strategy with driving homicide rates to historic lows and restoring public safety. Critics accuse Bukele's government of human-rights abuses, arbitrary detentions and erosion of due-process protections.
Salvadoran soldiers return to a base after El Salvador deployed thousands of troops to Haiti in response to four Salvadoran members of a UN-backed force that went missing in a gang ambush, in Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Oct. 30, 2026. (Patrice Noel/Reuters)
The question now is whether that model can be exported to Haiti, where gangs control large portions of Port-au-Prince and wield influence over key transportation routes and neighborhoods. Despite years of international intervention, security conditions have continued to deteriorate.
The GSF has struggled with manpower shortages and operational limitations, operating below its Security Council-approved intended strength, leaving Haiti's government unable to reassert full control over much of the capital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"We can help you defeat them, but we are not your enemies," Bukele wrote on Tuesday. "We must stand up, take back control of our communities, and put under our control those who are making us endure all this pain, all this suffering. We are right there beside you… Haiti will be free."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Tyler Speicher is an American journalist living in Slovenia after spending 25 years covering stories ranging from the Little League World Series to hurricanes, 9/11 and its aftermath for New York City news outlets, including 20 years on the Fox News Channel assignment desk.

articles.title_orig: A massive trade just happened in a leading mortgage lender
articles.title_zh: A massive trade just happened in a leading mortgage lender
articles.content_orig:
For more options-trading reaction to the rally, click the link at the top of the page for Options Action LIVE featuring CNBC contributors Michael Khouw and Brent Kochuba alongside host Oliver Renick.
Stocks are surging after midterms brought a Democratic blue wave and options traders are responding by selling volatility and embracing a rotation away from big-tech trades. The S&P 500 added just shy of 2% by midday Wednesday, recovering losses from Friday and Monday. The move in its corresponding options prices was even bigger, with the Cboe Volatility index falling about four points to below 17, the biggest one-day drop in the volatility gauge since at least July. Crude oil prices fell as WTI traded below $90 and energy stocks dropped 5.6% for the biggest decline in the S&P 500. Options on the State Street Energy Select Sector SPDR ETF (XLE) jumped to more than three times the 30-day average, with 57% puts by volume and the big-money trades concentrated in bearish put-buyers. The top trade in XLE was the 62.5-strike put expiring Jan. 15, suggesting it could be a slow rollover for what has been the best-performing sector of 2026, SpotGamma data show. With the drop in crude oil, a handful of inflation and interest-rate related trades got some bullish attention. Consumer discretionary stocks rallied almost 5% but options volume in the SPDR sector fund XLY was below average and volume was split between puts and calls, according to Cboe LiveVol data. Instead, there was some big action in a few housing trades such as Rocket Companies , the mortgage lender and Redfin owner that fell almost 50% this year before turning around last month. Options volume on Rocket was double the average with a strong bullish bias. Of the 110,000 options traded, 90% were calls and more were likely initiated by buyers than sellers. Bulls traded the bulls like the 14 and 16-strike calls expiring Nov. 20 the most. Opposite the drop in crude oil was a rally in solar energy companies, extending recent gains and extending unusual options activity that preceded the midterms. The Invesco Solar ETF (TAN) added another 9%, trading the highest since July. Options volume was more than five times the average and 80% of the volume was in calls. The most popular trade in TAN was the 48-strike call betting on a 6% rally through Nov. 20th. On the tech side, options flows looked bearish in the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) , which fell 2.6% to the lowest since May. Options volume was twice the average, 70% of it puts, with the 475-strike put expiring Nov. 13 the most popular contract bought by volume.

You can save a heck of lot of money on Google’s Pixel 11 phones through November 8th, whether you want the best-for-the-least Pixel 11 , or the slightly pricier Pixel 11 Pro that takes better photos. Even the big Pixel 11 Pro XL with a longer-lasting battery is hundreds off its original price.
The Pixel 11 Pro deal is the most attractive of the bunch, as the $1,099.99 phone with 256GB storage and 12GB of RAM is down to just $799.99 at Amazon , Best Buy , and at the Google Store , beating its October Prime Day price by $50. It’s $100 less than the base Pixel 11 model sold for at launch, and it’s the phone to get if you want great camera performance, plus extra features like HiLight that, while cool, weren’t really worth paying a premium to access. I’d be very surprised if the price dropped more for Black Friday.
There’s absolutely nothing wrong with opting for the Pixel 11 instead, especially at its attractive $699.99 ($200 off) price that now matches the cost of the iPhone 17E, following Apple’s September price bump . The Pixel 11 is the most affordable phone that supports Google’s software features that are exclusive to this year’s phones, including Magic Capture, Camera Looks, and Proactive Assistance. It has fast 25W wireless charging (up from 15W with the Pixel 10), and has 12GB of RAM, like the Pixel 11 Pro.
I’m still happily rocking my Pixel 9 Pro, but if I were going to upgrade right now, I’d get the Pixel 11 Pro. Yes, I want the better cameras and HiLight. But really, the main reason I’m lured to the Pro is because the trade-in offers are really generous right now. It’s just $10 more to opt for the Pro over the base Pixel 11. My base Pixel 9 Pro with 128GB of storage can fetch $530 in trade-in credit at the Google Store and $525 at Best Buy, which seems great.

articles.title_orig: Voters rebuff data centers in every ballot measure except one during the 2026 midterms
articles.title_zh: Voters rebuff data centers in every ballot measure except one during the 2026 midterms
articles.content_orig:
The artificial intelligence data center boom hit a roadblock on election night , further complicating the tech industry's historic expansion plans.
There were 41 local ballot measures in 10 states up for a vote on Tuesday that would place restrictions on the construction of data centers in different ways, according to Ballotpedia .
Voters sided against data centers in each measure except one in Harwood, North Dakota, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. The lone exception was Harwood, North Dakota, where voters rejected an added review of industrial projects, including data centers.
Ohio alone accounted for more than half of the measures, with 21 on the ballot. The issue also played out at the top of the ticket, where Democrat Sherrod Brown ousted Republican Sen. Jon Husted after casting the incumbent as "the face of data centers."
The Buckeye State, which was named America's Top State for Business in 2026 by CNBC, has become a key battleground for the issue.
OpenAI announced in August that it secured 8 gigawatts of computing capacity at the PORTS-Pike Technology Campus in Ohio, the largest planned AI data center campus in the world. The first phase of construction is slated to begin this year, and capacity is expected to come online in phases starting in 2028, according to the project's website .
SoftBank and SB Energy are developing the Ohio data center campus in partnership with the U.S. Department of Energy. SoftBank is a major investor in OpenAI, and the two companies announced plans to invest $1 billion in SB Energy earlier this year.
Nvidia is backstopping the project, which could cost more than $500 billion in total.
Those plans could now run into resistance from the governor's mansion. Ohio's top office flipped blue on Tuesday, as Democrat Amy Acton, a physician, defeated Republican businessman Vivek Ramaswamy. Acton supports a "conditional moratorium" on data centers to ensure they cover 100% of utility costs and "exclusively build with union labor."
Heading into the election, the AI trade was already faltering on Wall Street, with chipmakers, neoclouds and other data center-related companies selling off in October on concerns about rising interest rates and overspending. The hyperscalers — Alphabet , Amazon , Microsoft and Meta — are each spending hundreds of billions of dollars a year on AI infrastructure to meet what they say is insatiable demand. All of those companies except Microsoft have turned cash flow negative in the process.
Getting data center projects off the ground may have just gotten a lot harder.
Communities in California, Florida, Illinois, Kansas, Maine, New Jersey, Nevada and Wisconsin also went to the polls to weigh in on the issue, according to Ballotpedia, and data centers were a key motivating factor for voters in matters up and down the ballot.
In a CNBC Voter Poll, 56% of voters said data centers were a crucial or major factor in their decision, with Democrats ranking the issue higher than Republicans.
Democrats who campaigned on pausing or regulating new projects won key races in Ohio, Wisconsin, Georgia and Texas, which is on track to become the world's largest data center market by 2030.
In one of the most significant results of the night for Democrats, Gina Hinojosa unseated Gov. Greg Abbott after blaming the Republican incumbent for the rapid buildout of data centers across Texas, saying he put the tech industry's interests ahead of local communities.
The losses came despite record spending from Silicon Valley to shape the 2026 midterms, with the GOP boasting a commanding advantage among the election's biggest donors. According to a CNBC analysis of Federal Election Commission records, 14 of the 20 largest donor groups backed Republicans almost exclusively. Crypto, AI and online gambling interests poured in more than $377 million.
Elon Musk , the cycle’s largest individual donor, spent at least $474 million, nearly half of it in Texas, and lost both of the state’s marquee races. It was a warning sign for the wave of tech companies and founders who left California for Texas in search of a friendlier business climate.
"Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk wrote in a post on X.
Within hours of the polls closing, Democrats were already calling for AI executives to testify under oath.
Among the first to seize on the results was Rep. Greg Casar, the Texas Democrat who chairs the Congressional Progressive Caucus.
"The House Democratic majority must make it a top priority to protect Americans' jobs, freedom, and lives from AI billionaires," Casar said in a statement after Democrats were projected to win the House. "AI company CEOs should be called to testify under oath."
Casar also accused Republicans of being "bought and paid for by AI billionaires," arguing that voters had rejected that influence and warning Democrats to "hold them accountable instead of cashing their checks."
He said the data center fight is only the beginning.
"The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election," he said. "And in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics."
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the presumptive next chair of the House Oversight Committee, summed it up in two words: "Lawyer up."
— CNBC's Ashley Capoot contributed to this article.

articles.title_zh: As a Blue Wave Washes Over Washington, Trump Media Stock Heads for a Record Low
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Capitol building is seen on Nov. 4, 2026 in Washington, D.C.
Following two years of anti-climate legislation from Washington, Tuesday’s blue tidal wave —giving Democrats control of both the Senate and the House—could provide an opportunity to change course.
Following his 2024 reelection, President Trump withdrew from the Paris Agreement, rolled back the landmark endangerment finding , and leased public lands for oil and gas drilling—with Democrats unable to do much about it.
The next two years likely won’t bring aggressive climate policy , nonetheless a shift is expected as a result of the midterms . “Are we going to see ambitious climate action? The answer is no,” says Ken Gillingham, professor of environmental and energy economics at the Yale School of the Environment. “We still have an executive branch with a veto power controlled by President Trump, and so anything that is done would have to make it through the veto.”
But while Democrats might be unable to reverse many of the rollbacks, the midterms now give them, “a stronger hand to play,” says Geoffrey Henderson, assistant professor of environmental policy and planning at the University of Michigan.
One priority might be to reinstate billions of dollars in climate funding that President Trump has withheld. Chellie Pingree, a Democrat who won reelection in Maine, serves on the House Appropriations Committee and has said that she plans to force the administration to spend climate money.
Democrats also have the power to focus on bulking up the permitting reform bill, which aims to overhaul the permit process to speed up energy projects. The bill appeared likely to pass even before the election, but was filled with concessions. “Prior to the election, the bill included a number of provisions to weaken core environmental laws like the National Environmental Policy Act,” says Henderson. “What Democrats can now do is basically ask for a better deal.”
Increased support for domestic battery manufacturing is also likely—which could be a key part in meeting clean energy targets. “There would be an appetite for domestic onshoring of some of the supply chain that goes into electric vehicles, and I think that this is pretty bipartisan,” says Gillingham.
Gillingham also notes that we could see Democrats pursue “all of the above” climate policies, which often include oil and gas concessions along with clean energy growth.
“There's just not going to be an appetite among a whole set of members of the Democratic Caucus for ambitious climate action, even if they may be sympathetic to climate action, they don't have the political backing to do it from where they are sitting,” he notes. “But they do have the political backing to do all of the above energy policies.”
Democrats also achieved trifectas—controlling the House, Senate, and governorship—in Michigan, Wisconsin, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, and Nevada. In Pennsylvania, for example, this opens the floodgates to pass legislation to regulate data centers, allow community solar, and to require utilities to store excess electricity.
This election—in which energy affordability took center stage—also proved that climate change isn’t the taboo subject many have made it out to be.
“The results create new opportunities and give some breathing room to bring climate back into the energy discussion, especially if those discussions can deliver both economic benefits and emissions reductions, particularly around electricity affordability, grid infrastructure, and clean-energy investment,” Bethany Patten, executive director of the  MIT Climate Policy Center, said in an email.
Florida Democrat Kathy Castor, and Marcy Kaptur, an Ohio Democrat, are both candidates who did not give in to the “climate hushing” many other Democrats fell victim to. “Their victory suggests that being a vocal advocate for climate action is consistent with winning tough races, even in red states,” says Henderson. “Going forward, I think candidates should feel more empowered to talk about the issue.”

By The Maritime Executive 2026-11-03 16:05:55
Shipowners, managers and seafarers need to have a sense of where the risk of a resumption of the U.S.-Iran war currently sits, and putting aside temptations to be precise with regard to timing, the risk of a resumption of full-scale war could not be higher than it is now - and it will stay at that level for the next week. And the initiative to restart the war could be taken by Israel, Iran, the United States or even, conceivably, the Gulf states themselves.
From a political perspective, Prime Minister Netanyahu’s desire to resume hostilities has been advertised by his clashes with the Israeli chief of staff. President Trump may be tempted to do so before seats change hands in Congress. Iran is under increasing pressure domestically as the oil money runs out and imports dry up, and could leverage a patriotic war as a diversion. Some of the Gulf states do not want to see any arrangement come into play that gives Iran more control over the Strait of Hormuz than it used to have, and they might move if they were threatened with a fait accompli or a deal to which they were not a party.
From a military perspective, the United States has been clearing dependents and nonessential personnel from forward bases and embassies in the region, and it has mastered the art of prosecuting long-range warfare without giving away any indicators and warnings. Israel is always ready, and the fake full-scale attack mounted last week, which stopped just short of Iran’s borders, may have been an attempt to get the Iranians to unmask their air defense systems in order to update the electronic signatures of the systems that will need to be attacked.
Get the latest maritime news delivered to your inbox daily.
A series of covert, unannounced military strikes by the United States on targets in Iran in recent days may also be viewed as an attempt to prepare the battlefield, and unexplained fires and explosions at a number of sites in Iran could likewise be part of shaping operations.
Iran may want to avoid another war, knowing the damage that will be done to its infrastructure. But its leaders evidently feel a war is imminent and have been trying to pressure the Gulf states to urge restraint on the United States and Israel by threatening attacks on a wide range of civilian targets. But if Iran feels threatened and thinks an attack is imminent, it may be tempted to make a preemptive first move.

articles.title_orig: Hungary releases secret police files from communist era
articles.title_zh: Hungary releases secret police files from communist era
articles.content_orig:
The files were released on Wednesday as part of a campaign promise by Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar
Hungary has opened communist-era secret police files to the public, in a controversial move the government says will help Hungarian society heal itself from the traumas of 45 years of communist rule.
Critics say the move comes too late, that the files themselves are incomplete, and that the move risks sowing division and causing unnecessary anguish to family members.
The date of the opening is symbolic - on 4 November 1956 Soviet tanks rolled through Budapest and other cities, to crush Hungary's short-lived revolution.
"I ask everyone to treat this long overdue publication of documents with dignity and humanity,"  Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar told reporters at the state archives in Budapest.
"Many families will now face difficult information, often related to a deceased relative," he added. "It is impossible to process a trauma without discussion and asking questions."
Magyar defended the move, which was a central promise of his election campaign ahead of his landslide victory in April elections, as the fulfilment of a promise made by those who toppled the Communist party in 1989 in Hungary.
How the downfall of Serbia's VuÄiÄ mirrored that of Hungary's OrbÃ¡n
Hungarian MPs scrap OrbÃ¡n's anti-LGBTQ measures
In the ensuing decades, conservative, Socialist-Liberal, and Fidesz-led governments  have all contemplated, but ultimately refused to open the files.
Since 1998, it has been possible to apply for your own file, and for historians to research those of others. But many names were blacked out, and many files withheld by the post-communist secret services for their own use.
Over the past 36 years, there were frequent leaks of data from the files, as successive governments tried to damage their opponents. Many files were also shredded, as the Communist party lost its grip in 1988-89.
From Wednesday, the names and personal data of around 60,000 people recruited by the communist-era secret services have become available on the nyitottaktak.hu website , external .
So-called Form 6 cards have been released (above) showing people's full details, but B-dossiers detailing recruitment registers will come next February
A typical entry records the real name of the informer, their codename, date of birth, address and mother's name, their motive for recruitment - whether voluntary or because they were blackmailed or coerced - and the name of their handling officer.
Another batch of files, known as the "B-dossiers" are currently being digitalised, and will be made available on 25 February.
These will offer much more detail about the recruitment process, and the high or low value of the information they provided.
Critics of the opening of the files emphasise this point - that people will be too quick to judge those they find in the files, and unwilling to understand the nuances.
Around 150-160,000 people are estimated to have been recruited as informers between December 1944 and February 1990 in Hungary.
Many were blackmailed, with threats including loss of work or study opportunities, loss of access to medicines, or the leaking of information about their sex lives or addictions. Such intimate details will be carefully edited out of the current disclosures too.
Krisztian UngvÃ¡ry, a historian who has long campaigned for full public access to the files, says access to information on what is recorded by the state against the citizen is a citizens' right, and should not depend on the whims of those in power.
"In the overwhelming majority of surviving agent reports, it isn't even possible to identify the agent, let alone their motives," counters an opponent of today's move, Zsuzsanna BorvendÃ©g, a historian and MEP of the far-right Our Homeland party.
Publishing the names of informers without fully explaining the circumstances of their recruitment and their activities risks misleading the public, she told Hungarian media.

articles.title_orig: Oil Prices Sink as U.S. Midterms Raise Market Hopes for Middle East Solution
articles.title_zh: Oil Prices Sink as U.S. Midterms Raise Market Hopes for Middle East Solution
articles.content_orig:
Oil prices fell on Wednesday in a volatile session ​as investors awaited Washington's next move in ​the US-Israeli war on ​Iran, after Democrats captured control of Congress from President Donald Trump's Republicans in the midterm elections.
Brent futures fell 2.5% to $101.02 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell 2.6% to $93.61.
In the previous session, Brent settled at its lowest level in ⁠nearly four weeks as traders weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran.
President Donald Trump acknowledged that the US-Israeli war on Iran played a role in his party's sweeping defeat in the midterm elections, as Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate.
"President ‌Trump's conflicting signals, with military strikes continuing alongside statements downplaying further escalation, have made it difficult for traders to build strong directional conviction," said Priyanka Sachdeva, head of market insights at Phillip Nova, adding ​that profit-taking and a reduction in speculative long positions were justified after the sharp rally in October.
The US had carried out "defensive" strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island targeting surface-to-air missiles used against US assets, a US official said on Tuesday.
Markets remained on watch for any progress in talks to end the US-Israeli war with ⁠Iran, as Qatar stepped up mediation efforts to avert an escalation of attacks after the US elections. A senior Iranian official told Reuters ‌on Tuesday that Iran and the United States remain far from a deal ‌to end their war.
US President Donald Trump told the Financial Times on Tuesday that the United States had no immediate plans to strike Iran.
Meanwhile flows of crude, condensate and refined products, excluding LPG, averaged 17.1 million barrels per day in October, according to ship-tracking data ⁠from Vortexa, marking a drop from 18.9 million bpd in September but still representing roughly three-quarters of pre-war ⁠levels.
"The continued recovery in crude shipments from the Middle East has begun to weigh on physical ⁠cargo prices, potentially helping to accelerate the normalisation of refining margins and, ultimately, lower fuel prices," said Saxo Bank analyst Ole Hansen.
"However, for consumers to feel the full benefit, refined product exports ​from Middle Eastern refineries must also recover. So far, this ‌is one area where the rebound in flows remains notably subdued, suggesting that relief at the pump may take longer to materialise."
In the US, crude stocks fell by 5.27 million barrels in the week ended October 30, market sources said on Wednesday, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Eight analysts polled by Reuters had expected, on average, a rise of about 880,000 barrels in crude ​inventories.
Official data from the US Energy Information Administration is ‌due at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) on Wednesday.
