articles.title_orig: AI Data Center Boom Set for Upheaval After US Election Rout
articles.title_zh: AI Data Center Boom Set for Upheaval After US Election Rout
articles.content_orig:
It was a bad night for data centers . In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown, who has aired ads for months calling his opponent “the face of data centers in Ohio,” cruised to victory to flip a Senate seat. Democrat Chris Pappas, who when seated will be the nation’s first openly gay male senator, mentioned his opposition to data centers in his victory speech and drew massive boos from his crowd in New Hampshire—even though the state has no large-scale data centers under construction.
Elsewhere, two separate Republicans named Derek and Derrick, whose Democratic opponents labeled them “Data Center Derek” and “DC Derrick,” suffered losses in House races in Ohio and Wisconsin.
As part of last night’s shocking blue tsunami , voters selected candidates with tough policies on data centers at all levels of government, in a clear rebuke to the industry’s buildout in states across the country. Almost a quarter of all voters told NBC News that data centers were “crucial” to their vote, while nearly two-thirds said it was either a major or minor factor.
“The revolt against data centers was one of the top issues of the 2026 election, and in a few years we will look back on it as just the early tremor of a much bigger AI earthquake upending American politics,” Greg Casar, the Texas Democratic congressman, said in a statement .
“Data centers and AI as a technology are fundamentally linked in many voters' minds,” says Alexander McCoy, a Democratic strategist working on AI. “So you can address all of the different concerns with data centers with regards to their energy or their noise, or their pollution, and there would still be significant concerns about what these projects are enabling and the effect is having on opportunities, prices, jobs, society.”
Perhaps some of the biggest shocks for the industry came in the governor’s mansions. In stunning upsets, voters elected Democrats Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Gina Hinojosa in Texas, while putting Cindy Holscher on the cusp of a potential win in Kansas. All of these candidates campaigned not just for increased regulations on the industry, but for data center moratoriums. A pause on data centers in Texas and Georgia especially, two of the biggest hubs for development in the country, could have serious implications for the hundreds of projects planned for each of those states.
“I think we will see the end to favorable tax breaks, and it’s clear that people like Greg Abbott were harmed by their history of giving those financial incentives to AI companies and data center developers,” says McCoy. “I think we'll likely see the appointment of regulators in various administrative bureaucratic bodies that pose more scrutiny on these projects and an increase in the enforcement of environmental protection regulations.”
Simply being anti-data center wasn’t enough to boost some candidates—especially Republicans. In Wisconsin, Republican Tom Tiffany, who hit Democrat David Crowley early on in his campaign with ads dubbing him “Data Center David Crowley,” lost his race. (Crowley got more aggressive on the industry as the campaign went on, indicating he would support a pause two weeks before election day.) So did incumbent Mike Lawler in New York’s 17th congressional district, who aired ads slamming his opponent’s past statements that New York “needs” data centers, conceded his race even though the Associated Press has yet to call it.
Throughout the campaign, data centers proved to be a bipartisan topic of concern , and caused fractures within the parties themselves. Earlier this year, WIRED reported how many of Donald Trump’s MAGA loyalists disagreed with the president’s support for AI companies and data centers.
But it’s undeniable that anger about data centers helped elect Democrats. In the weeks leading up to the elections, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee ran ads that highlighted Republicans’ support for data centers or the backing they had received from AI companies.
“Voters aren’t stupid. The data center story is a corruption story. It's an affordability story. It's a Big Tech CEOs influence story,” says Sacha Haworth executive director of the Tech Oversight Project. “That's what voters understood when they cast their ballots and that's why Democrats routed Republicans so, so hard last night, because Republicans could not tell the same story.”
Many of the candidates who won on stricter data center regulations did so despite massive injections of cash from the AI and data center industries to their opponents. In South Carolina, Building the Future, a new industry super PAC, spent $1.5 million to support Darline Graham; she lost last night to Democrat Annie Andrews, who favors a moratorium. (Andrews registered the URL DataCenterDarline.com in late September to hit Graham on her industry connections.) Building the Future also injected more than $1.5 million into the Kansas gubernatorial race to support Republican Ty Masterson against Holscher. And Michigan Democrat Will Lawrence, who made regulations on AI and data centers a cornerstone of his campaign, has declared victory (though without an AP announcement) over Republican Tom Barrett in one of the most expensive races in the country. Barrett had gotten $340,000 from Elon Musk’s America PAC over the course of the race.
“Despite poll after poll making it clear that the conservative rural working-class base was concerned about data centers and the impact of AI, too many politicians in Washington chose big AI’s money over their own base,” Amy Kremer, chair of Humans First, an advocacy group pushing for democratic oversight of AI, said in a statement.
In data center ballot measures across nine states, voters rejected future construction plans, approved moratoriums, and called for greater consultation with and accountability to local communities. Ten states put forth more than 40 questions about data centers on local ballots, according to Ballotpedia, including 21 in Ohio alone. Questions ranged from outright moratoriums to rezoning questions to restrictions on development. Just one county appears to have allowed for more data center development on their ballot, according to Americans for Responsible Innovation president Brad Carson, who was tracking ballot developments throughout the night.
Tech companies appear to be smelling blood in the water. On the day of the midterms, The Hill reported that environmental groups and Big Tech companies were working together as part of a “Responsible Data Center Development Collaborative” to create a framework for data center development. McCoy calls this kind of collaboration the “right next step.”
Meanwhile, as the results rolled in, Musk posted on X , “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

articles.title_orig: Dow futures rally 700 points as Democrats win big in midterms: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow futures rally 700 points as Democrats win big in midterms: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stock futures ripped higher on Wednesday, reversing earlier losses, as a decisive victory by Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections allowed investors to look past the political risk hanging over the market.
Futures tied to the Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 724 points, or 1.4%. S&P 500 futures traded 1% higher, along with Nasdaq-100 futures . Stock futures were down sharply overnight.
Democrats took control of Congress Tuesday night, winning majorities in both the House and Senate. They also scored victories in key gubernatorial races, including Texas.
Heading into the election investors worried a Democratic sweep could weigh on some areas of the market , especially stocks related to the artificial intelligence build-out. Wall Street also worried that a clear winner would not emerge Tuesday night. However, those concerns eased after President Donald Trump said he was willing to accept the election results and work with Democrats.
Elon Musk's SpaceX was down 4.8% in premarket trading, while Tesla shares shed 4.9%. Neocloud stocks CoreWeave and Nebius fell 3.6% and 1%, respectively.
But other parts of the tech trade gained. Microsoft advanced 0.3%, and Amazon climbed 1.1%, as Nvidia moved 0.5% higher. Alphabet was the outlier, trading around 0.4% lower.
U.S. health insurers and hospital operators also advanced, with United Health up 1.4%, Molina Healthcare rising 6.3%, Centene adding 4.7% and HCA Healthcare up 1.44%.
Renewables stocks rallied sharply in premarket trading, while defense stocks fell.
AMD shares popped 6% after the chipmaker reported third-quarter earnings and revenue that blew past analyst expectations.
Andrew Slimmon of Morgan Stanley Investment Management said the result will bring "gridlock" to Washington, but added that the markets "like gridlock — they don't like a party with too much power."
Speaking with CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe", Slimmon said that if the result increases the push for a resolution to the Middle East conflict, that may bring oil prices lower.  "That's been an issue for the Fed, and inflation, and part of the reason that rates are higher."
Renewable shares like solar stocks traded higher in the post-market on speculation a Democratic majority in Congress would halt policies by President Donald Trump taken against the industry. The Invesco Solar ETF was up 3% in Robinhood trading.
President Donald Trump may have helped ease pressure on the market a bit overnight by not challenging the midterm results in an interview with the Wall Street Journal . Trump told the WSJ, "I think we'll work with the Democrats, and we'll get along very well with them."
Nasdaq-100 futures are up 929.75 points off their overnight lows, based on the current price of 28,545.50. Futures contracts tied to the benchmark hit a low of 27,615.75,  their lowest since July 30.
Precious metals saw strong gains on Wednesday morning as the Democrats scored a clean sweep in the midterm elections, flipping both the House and Senate.
Spot gold was 2.93% higher at $4,043.45 an ounce by 5:05 a.m. ET, while spot silver jumped 4.44% to trade at $51.98 per ounce, as traders reacted to the U.S. midterm election results.
Front-month gold futures added 2.9% to trade at $4,054.60, while silver futures were up 4.64% at $52.09.
Other metals seeing notable gains on Wednesday morning included platinum , which jumped 2.47% to trade at $1,465.30, and palladium, which was 5.93% higher at $989.
Renewables and healthcare shares are among the biggest premarket movers, trading higher after Democrats took control of the House and Senate. Meanwhile, neocloud stocks, as well as prison operators and defense names, lag the broader market.
U.S. renewable energy stocks climbed on expectations of a policy shift. First Solar advanced 8.5%, Bloom Energy gained 5.8%, Plug Power rose 10.6%, Sunrun notched an 8.64% gain, FuelCell Energy was up 6.24% and SolarEdge Technologies moved 4% higher.
Healthcare stocks also rose. UnitedHealth gained 1.8%, Molina Healthcare added 6.3%, Centene climbed 5% and HCA Healthcare advanced 7.16%.
Neocloud stocks, in contrast, turned lower, with CoreWeave down 3.6% and Nebius off 1%. Shares of prison operators and defense names also fell.
European renewable energy stocks moved sharply higher in early trade as prospects of a decisive Democrat victory in the U.S. midterm elections sparked hopes of a U.S. policy shift on renewables.
Copenhagen-listed Oersted surged 7.3% while Danish peer Vestas advanced 5.2%. The two companies have grappled with uncertainty in their U.S. businesses in recent years, partly as a result of fierce opposition from the Trump administration toward the renewable energy sector.
SMA Solar shares were up 5.5% and Nordex shares added 4.8%.
The pan-European Stoxx 600 added 0.44% in early trading, as the continent's stocks and major bourses moved higher on the Democrats' clean sweep of the U.S. midterms.
Banks advanced 1.83%, leading gains, with basic resources up 1.71% and utilities rising 0.68%. Food and beverage stocks lost 0.57%, and industrial goods fell 0.37%.
The Italian FTSE MIB was up 0.88%, leading regional bourses. The U.K.'s FTSE 100 added 0.22%, while the French CAC 40 rose 0.24% and Germany's DAX gained 0.28%.
Novo posted quarterly earnings ahead of expectations early Wednesday as sales of its Wegovy pill blew past estimates amid continued GLP-1 volume growth globally, sending shares up as much as 6% in early trading.
The company updated its outlook to now see adjusted revenue and operating profit growth between negative 2% and 2% at constant exchange rates. It previously saw full-year sales and operating profits, which it hiked in August, at negative 6% to flat for both metrics.
Sales in the third quarter came in at 79.2 billion Danish kroner ($11.9 billion), up 4% year-on-year at constant exchange rates and ahead of FactSet estimates of 73.6 billion kroner. Adjusted operating profit (EBIT) was 31.7 billion kroner, compared with the expected 28.6 billion kroner.
It comes as the Danish weight-loss drug maker is looking to regain momentum following a tumultuous year in which it fell behind rival Eli Lilly.
Asia-Pacific markets closed mixed Wednesday, as investors assessed a projected Democratic takeover of the U.S. Senate and House, while President Donald Trump appeared to not challenge the results.
"We'll work with the Democrats, and we'll get along very well with them," Trump told the Wall Street Journal.
South Korea's Kospi rose 0.62% to end at 5,683.8, while the small-cap, tech-focused Kosdaq added 1.5% to 714.95 in choppy trading.
Japan's Nikkei 225 pared some losses to close 1.42% lower at 62,188.63, and the broad-based Topix declined 0.89% to 3,895.38.
Mainland China's CSI 300 gained 2.31% to 4,101.34, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was 1.43% higher in its last hour of trade.
Australia's S&P/ASX 200 fell 0.59% to 8,834.5.
— Lee Ying Shan, Lim Hui Jie
The dollar moved lower against most major currencies as the Democrats took control of Congress after the U.S. midterm elections.
The euro was last seen 0.39% higher against the dollar at $1.1235, while the British pound also strengthened against the greenback, rising 0.48% to $1.3476.
The dollar index , which tracks the greenback's strength against a basket of six major currencies, was down 0.39% at $101.32.
Treasury yields moved lower on Wednesday as investors sought shelter from a sell-off in equity futures sparked by potential big victories from Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections.
The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield was last seen 1 basis point lower at 4.9311%. The 30-year bond yield slipped 1 basis point to 5.3136%, and the shorter-term 2-year note yield pulled back 1 basis point to 4.6017%.
European stock markets are set to open negative as investors respond to overnight projections of a major Democratic victory in the U.S. midterms.
The Democrats are projected to win both chambers of Congress, according to The Associated Press.

articles.title_orig: China calls for constructive ties with US amid Democratic gains in midterm elections
articles.title_zh: China calls for constructive ties with US amid Democratic gains in midterm elections
articles.content_orig:
The Democratic Party has regained control of the lower chamber of the United States Congress, winning the House of Representatives.
Late on Tuesday night local time, the House result was called in favour of the left-wing party.
Democrats needed to gain five seats to flip the chamber. Republicans have held a majority in the House since the 2022 midterms, during the presidency of Democrat Joe Biden.
The outgoing 119th House has 218 Republicans, 214 Democrats, one independent and two vacancies.
All 435 seats in the House were up for grabs in the election. A term in the House lasts only two years, compared with six for the Senate.
The Democrats’ victory in the House means their party leader in the chamber, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, will likely be selected as the speaker, the chamber’s top officer.
That position would make Jeffries the third in line for the US presidency, should the president and the vice president be removed from office.
He would also be the first Black person to serve in the role. He will replace outgoing Republican Speaker Mike Johnson of Louisiana, who has held the post since 2023.
Democrats had been widely projected to regain control of the House, leveraging backlash to the second administration of President Donald Trump, which saw record-low approval ratings in the weeks leading up to the midterms.
For the last two years, Trump’s Republican Party has held a political “trifecta” in Washington, DC, with control of the presidency and both chambers of Congress. The 120th Congress is slated to be sworn in on January 3, 2027.
Democrats swept Republican-held House seats on their way to retaking the chamber.
In Iowa, Democrat Sarah Trone Garriott unseated Republican Zach Nunn in the state’s 3rd Congressional District.
In Virginia, Democrat Elaine Luria won a tight race against Republican incumbent Jen Kiggans, while in Pennsylvania’s 10th Congressional District, Democrat Janelle Stelson unseated seven-term Republican Scott Perry.
Meanwhile, Democrat incumbents Ilhan Omar and Ro Khanna sailed to victory, holding on to their seats in Minnesota and California.
Reacting to the Democratic wave, former President Barack Obama said the results showed voters wanted leaders who would bring people together and offer solutions to the problems they face.
“Tonight, the American people sent a clear message,” Obama wrote on X. He praised candidates who ran in areas long considered difficult for Democrats to win and urged supporters to keep organising during Trump’s remaining two years in office.
Senator Bernie Sanders said Democratic control of both chambers would allow the party to “hold Trump accountable”.
He urged Democrats to tackle income and wealth inequality. “We must aggressively fight for working families. No more excuses,” Sanders said.
Even Trump issued rare praise for the Democratic campaign in an interview with Fox News.
“I think the Democrats did a good job. I really do. I think they did a good job. They fought hard,” the president said.

articles.title_orig: Stocks, dollar slide as stunning victories for Democrats jolt AI bets
articles.title_zh: Stocks, dollar slide as stunning victories for Democrats jolt AI bets
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
SINGAPORE, Nov 4 (Reuters) - Global stocks slumped and the dollar hit a one-month low on Wednesday as Democrats gained control of both the Senate and the House in the US midterm elections, fuelling fears that rapid AI sector growth could be hamstrung by regulatory scrutiny.
In ‌a major setback to President Donald Trump, Democrats notched up victories in the South Carolina, Texas and Ohio Senate races, capturing majorities in both the ‌Senate and House that reached deep into Republican strongholds.
The breadth of the party's success was underscored by gains in districts long considered safely conservative, highlighting a political shift that caught many investors off guard.
AI stocks ​were quick to slide. That in turn put the dollar under pressure, while cryptocurrencies also fell at the prospect of stronger regulations. Bonds, though, found favour as investors sought safer assets.
"Tighter regulatory scrutiny of technology and AI companies along with the higher likelihood of political gridlock beckon with a Democrat sweep," said Prashant Newnaha, senior rates strategist at TD Securities in Singapore.
The AI boom has helped propel global markets in recent years, driven by heavy spending from tech giants racing to build data centres and expand computing capacity. That has ‌left investors acutely sensitive to anything that could derail the ⁠technology's rapid expansion.
The election outcome could also hold broad implications for the US fiscal outlook as well as sectors such as defence, healthcare and banking.
S&P 500 futures were last down 0.35% while Nasdaq futures skidded more than 2% before cutting losses to trade down 0.5%. ⁠European futures were down 0.4%, having slid 1.5% earlier.
"Looks like investors are buying the dip after the initial knee-jerk selloff," said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo. "The blue sweep hasn't changed, but markets may be recognising that political gridlock doesn't necessarily mean weaker corporate earnings."
In Asia, the bulk of selling was in AI stocks, with chipmakers Samsung, SK Hynix and TSMC sliding ​sharply ​before cutting losses. The KOSPI was last slightly higher after dropping 3% earlier.
George Efstathopoulos, portfolio manager ​and co-head of multi-asset research at Fidelity International, said he had ‌reduced overall equity exposure and dialled up exposure in defensive sectors like utilities, but thinks now is a good time to gradually rotate back into tech.
"The midterms are a clearing event that can allow investors to focus on sectors where fundamentals and pricing have diverged. Technology is one of them."
INVESTORS RUSH FOR SAFETY OF BONDS
Treasuries rallied as investors expect gridlock in Washington to cut government spending. AI regulation could also slow growth and reduce the need for rate hikes.
The yield on the benchmark US 10-year Treasury note fell 6 basis points to 4.906%, pushing the dollar sharply lower. [FRX/] [US/]
"Bonds are coming out as the clear winner as markets put the AI trade on the chopping block ‌and embrace the higher possibility that further tax cuts are put on ice and government spending ​slows," said TD Securities' Newnaha.
Kim Seok-hwan, an analyst at Mirae Asset Securities, said the Democrats' victory in ​Texas is likely to weigh on chip stocks, raising fears of tighter ​curbs on AI data-centre development in one of the fastest-growing markets for computing infrastructure in the US.
"If Texas declares a moratorium on data ‌centres, as New York did, projects could face further delays," Kim ​said. "Today's market reaction is clearly reflecting concerns ​and uncertainty over these issues."
In currencies, the dollar slid broadly against major peers. The euro rose 0.5% to $1.1249, while sterling firmed 0.37% to $1.3464. That left the dollar index 0.37% lower at 101.34. [FRX/]
The yen and the Swiss franc — both safe-haven currencies — notched up the biggest gains. The yen was 0.7% stronger at 157.55 ​per US dollar, while the Swiss franc firmed almost 0.8% ‌to 0.8144 per US dollar.
In the oil market, prices were choppy on Wednesday after sliding to a four-week low in the previous session as ​investors weighed talks to end the wars in Ukraine and Iran against worries that recent attacks in both conflicts could further disrupt supplies. [O/R]
(Reporting by ​Ankur Banerjee and Rae Wee in Singapore; Editing by Shri Navaratnam and Christopher Cushing)

articles.title_orig: Democrats seize Congress in sweeping midterm repudiation of Trump
articles.title_zh: Democrats seize Congress in sweeping midterm repudiation of Trump
articles.content_orig:
Xi urges diplomacy on Iran as Oman’s sultan makes historic visit to China
Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia – Across the Asia-Pacific region, governments and businesses reeling from the energy shock of the United States and Israel’s war on Iran are watching Tuesday’s US midterm elections closely.
Many want to see “enormous changes” during the rest of President Donald Trump’s term, analysts say, from the war on Iran to his policies on trade and tariffs. But few expect that to happen, even with the Democrats poised to take the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate, from Trump’s Republican Party.
“Of course, everybody is watching,” said Steven Okun, a trade specialist and the chief executive of APAC Advisors, a Singapore-based consulting firm. “It’s great political theatre.”
Outside the Middle East, no region has been hit harder by the war on Iran than the Asia-Pacific. Before the start of the conflict in January, the region took in most of the Gulf oil and gas that passed through the Strait of Hormuz.
When Iran closed the chokepoint in response to the US and Israel’s strikes, much of the region was left facing shortages .
The Philippines, which relies on the Gulf for more than 90 percent of its crude oil imports, has been under a national energy emergency since March. Soaring fuel costs have drained the foreign exchange reserves of the region’s poorest economies – Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor, according to the Institute of Southeast Asian Studies (ISEAS)-Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore. Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Vietnam have also spent heavily on fuel subsidies to shield consumers, it said.
Public opinion in the US and the Asia-Pacific region remains firmly opposed to the war, but Okun said a Democratic-controlled US Congress was unlikely to force Trump to end the eight-month conflict.
“With Iran, I don’t see [a Democrat-controlled Congress] having much change at all, other than the fact that the war will be investigated and there will be oversight hearings,” Okun told Al Jazeera. “We might even see an impeachment of the secretary of defence, but it doesn’t change the overall impact of the war.”
Under the US Constitution, Congress holds the power to formally declare war, but Trump has claimed the attacks on Iran were in self-defence and has so far ignored congressional resolutions directing him to withdraw US forces from hostilities. If a Democrat-controlled Congress passes legislation restricting military operations or cutting funding for them, Trump can veto it.
Overriding a veto requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers, which Democrats are almost certain to fall short of.
On trade and tariffs, too, analysts see little room for Congress to rein in Trump.
The US president rattled global markets last year when he imposed “reciprocal” tariffs of 10 percent to 50 percent on some 90 countries, with the aim of shrinking the US trade deficit. The Asia Pacific was again hit harder than most. Some 15 countries were hit with tariffs, with Cambodia facing a 49 percent tariff and Laos 48 percent. Vietnam was slapped with 46 percent and Myanmar 45 percent.
After the Supreme Court struck down those tariffs in February, the Trump administration turned to other tools . In July, it imposed tariffs of 10 percent and 12.5 percent on goods from 60 trading partners, accusing them of failing to stop imports made with forced labour . In Asia, the list includes China, Japan, South Korea and seven Southeast Asian nations – Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.
“In some ways, the new Congress is not going to matter to the Asia Pacific because it’s not going to affect trade policy,” Okun said. “Congress cannot change that … Tariffs don’t change. The war doesn’t change.”
Still, some analysts see a narrow opening on tariffs.
Stephen Olson, a visiting fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, argued in a recent essay that a “strong rebuke of ‘Trumpism’” at the polls could embolden a pro-free-trade wing of the Republican Party that has been “intimidated into standing down during the Trump presidency”.
That, Olson wrote, offers “a glimmer of hope” for Southeast Asian countries that depend on the US market. A Democratic-controlled Congress, he said, could also push for carve-outs and exceptions that would give the region’s exporters “a modicum of relief”. But any deeper shift in US trade policy, he added, will have to wait for the 2028 presidential election.
Joshua Kurlantzick, a senior fellow for Southeast Asia and South Asia at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the region’s wish list goes beyond trade to security.
“I think nearly all of Asia would like to see enormous changes, across many domains, during the rest of Trump’s term,” he told Al Jazeera. “But I think much of the region believes this will not happen.”
Besides “more stability” in trade and tariff policy, Asia-Pacific countries “would like to feel more stable in security guarantees from the US,” he said. They would also like a “more clear, obvious US presence” in the South China Sea , where China’s claims overlap with those of five Southeast Asian nations, and in the Taiwan Strait , which separates China from Taiwan , the self-governed island Beijing claims as its territory.
Businesses will also be watching whether a major Republican loss leads to “greater GOP willingness in Congress to stand up to Trump, along with Democrats, on issues important to companies in Asia,” Kurlantzick said, including tariffs, trade policy, arms sales and “overall economic unpredictability”.
One area where analysts do expect Congress to act is on China.
The new Congress, whichever party controls it, will pass tougher restrictions on China’s access to technology, said Okun at APAC Advisors.
These include the Remote Access Security Act, which would extend export controls to remote access of US goods, software or technology and the Chip Security Act, which would require companies to verify that advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips remain in authorised locations, to prevent diversion to foreign adversaries. It also includes the Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, known as the MATCH Act, which would press allies to bring their controls on chipmaking equipment in line with Washington’s, to keep advanced chipmaking technology out of China’s hands.
“The next Congress is going to pass them regardless of midterms because both parties agree on them,” Okun said. “The person who is least restrictive now on China is the US president,” he added, referring to Trump’s courting of China’s President Xi Jinping.
The two men have met twice this year as ties have warmed after a bitter and costly trade war last year. To preserve the fragile trade truce, Trump has also held off approving a $14bn package of arms sales to Taiwan, which would be the largest ever for Taipei.
Some analysts meanwhile worry that a lame-duck Trump, hemmed in at home by a Democratic Congress, could turn more forcefully to foreign policy.
“We should not be surprised by continued erratic foreign policy,” said James Guild, an assistant professor at the Indonesian International Islamic University.
“The Democrats have a poor record of effectively opposing and holding Trump accountable using conventional tools of congressional oversight,” Guild said. “We will have to wait and see if they rise to the moment this time.”
